In view of the recent arrest in South Africa of Reverend Tom Anthony, director of the Canadian Anglican Church's national and overseas mission, along with 52 South African clergymen, and given that these arrests have taken place at a time when clergymen from around the world are meeting in South Africa and have stated their opposition to apartheid at some considerable personal risk, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling):

subsubtopic: PLANS OF ACTION TO REDUCE SHIP-BRIDGE COLLISIONS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of growing urgency to many parts of Canada. There have been over 20 major collisions between ships in motion and standing structures since 1965, resulting in large loss of life and countless millions in costs. Every day of delay by the federal and other levels of government in providing fendering protection for bridge piers brings us a day closer to a major disaster, one which could be significantly reduced if not eliminated. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby):
That this House regrets and condemns the Minister of Transport's failure to bring together the appropriate authorities for the purpose of developing plans of action to reduce the ever-growing danger of a major disaster.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to put forward a motion which should gain the full support of the House.
When this country joined the boycott of the Moscow Olympic Games we asked for the support of the athletes and they have given that support, in many instances at great sacrifice to themselves. Now we hear that in some instances national organizations or associations are not competing at a national level to determine national champions at a time when successful athletes should be so recognized and honoured.

CONSTITUTION OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO QUESTION SENATE MINISTERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the present system of appointing members of the Senate as ministers responsible for various departments denies elected members of the House of Commons the opportunity to question and pursue matters which are of direct concern to their constituencies, and whereas the present system of twinning a minister from the other place with one in the Commons results in the minister who answers in the Commons being nothing more than a messenger boy, which denies members of the House of Commons an opportunity to pursue a question where answers are vague or incomplete, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson):
That the Prime Minister institute a system whereby ministers who serve from the other place may appear at least once a week before a special sitting of a parliamentary committee constituted specifically to have these ministers appear before that committee, whose sole purpose would be to provide elected members the opportunity to question them on day to day operations of their respective departments.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question because the minister very clearly articulated his reservations about the leadership in the United States today. 1 would like to go on further. In another part of that same interview the minister gave his view that the United States is at least partly to blame for the current crisis in Afghanistan in that it failed to counter the activities of the Soviet Union in Afghanistan some two years ago. I find it passing strange that the minister should condemn the United States for something it did not do two years ago when he, as minister, took two months to summon up courage to introduce a boycott of the Olympic Games following the invasion of Afghanistan by Soviet troops.
Can the Prime Minister explain why the minister is now levelling his criticism at the United States rather than against those who are butchering children in Kabul?

speechtext: Here again, Madam Speaker, I think it is important that we look at the whole answer rather than just a part. The minister was not singling out any one country for criticism. He made it quite specific that he was talking about all the western powers. He talked about a mistake on the West's part.

speechtext: He was indicating, with the benefit of hindsight, that it might have been better if indeed the West had a couple of years ago, to use his own expression, been more concerned when the satellite government was first set up in Afghanistan about two years ago. So I would not want the hon. lady to think that the minister was directing his criticism at the United States particularly. He was appealing to the West generally to be more vigilant against Soviet aggression.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

If the Prime Minister would take the time to read that statement, he would see that it says "and especially by the United States," which the minister did single out.
Then there is another comment which I would like him to explain, if he would. The minister said that the Soviet Union's policies were to look for weak points, that they picked them off, but they do not go against the heart of western civilization, of western Europe. Given that Canada has consistently argued over the years that detente is indivisible, that military adventurism by the Soviet Union in other countries indeed has a bearing on the pursuit of detente in western Europe, am I to assume, then, from the minister's statement that it is now the
position of the Government of Canada that Soviet aggression elsewhere in the world against any neutral, non-aligned or Third World country will no longer have a bearing on the pursuit of detente in Europe?

Not at all, Madam Speaker. If once again the hon. lady looks at the question, she will see that the minister was indicating that this is not happening in Europe because there is some balance of power there. 1 think he would agree with the hon. lady that the danger is in other parts of the world where such a balance of power does not exist, where, to use his own words, they attempt adventures-
-and are more likely to attack a country like Pakistan or a country like Iran than they are to attempt an adventure in western Europe.
He was indicating that, because of the balance of force in Europe and because of NATO in particular, western Europe was not as endangered as were other parts of the world on which the Soviet Union was putting pressure.

1 have one final supplementary question, Madam Speaker. Just so that everyone will know that we are reading from the same transcript, I should like to quote the next line, which the Prime Minister refused to do, where he said that the Soviets are much more likely to attack a country like Pakistan or a country like Iran than they are to attempt an adventure in western Europe. I think that's completely out of the question.
Will the Prime Minister tell us on what certainty the Secretary of State for External Affairs is able to base his comment that Soviet aggression against western Europe is entirely, completely out of the question? If that is the case, why do we have NATO forces, a NATO alliance? What have we been doing in this last number of years except making sure that we are indeed ready in the event of an invasion of western Europe?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in light of the reply of the Minister of State for Finance, 1 should like to address a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Indeed, the official figures show that the leading economic indicators have plunged 4.8 per cent in one month, which is the largest decline ever registered on this particular set of indicators since they were started 32 years ago. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister. It deals with national security. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN CERTAIN MILITARY ALLIANCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member was not in the House at that time, but I should like to remind him that in the early seventies, or at the end of the sixties, we undertook to review our external policy and our military policy, with a view to re-examining Canada's membership in all those alliances, of which NATO and NORAD. This study was sincere and lasted quite a while; a large number of citizens and parliamentarians took part in it. speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to inform hon. members of the programs the government is putting into place to deal with the immediate employment needs of Canadians, and to discuss briefly employment development in the 1980s.
Canada is, above all, a land of contrasts. In some areas, such as those relating to our ethnic roots and traditions, diversity is a source of national strength. This is not the case with the diversities in our economic well-being. The existence of groups of Canadians who are continually frustrated in their yearning to participate fully in the economic life of Canada is a condition that weakens us as a nation.
In designing our employment program, we looked first at the principles that would provide the basis for specific initia-

June 2, 1980
Employment Strategy
tives. The first of these principles is the principle of targeting, or reaching out directly to those who traditionally receive little or no benefit from the economic growth of the country.
Native people, even in the very wealthy province of Alberta, face unemployment rates of approximately 75 per cent, and this situation is even more critical for native women. Handicapped people everywhere face not only the challenge of overcoming their disability, but also must contend with the invisible barriers of prejudice and ignorance that bar their entry into the labour force. Women, and particularly those who have worked tirelessly in their homes to raise families, are told that they are not wanted in the paid labour force. Whatever else we do to ensure that all Canadians enjoy rising levels of real income, we must give special assistance to such people as I have mentioned.
The second principle upon which today's measures are based is the recognition that employment must have continuing and genuine value. It should offer an unemployed worker hope for the future, and contribute to his or her sense of self-worth. In the programs we are announcing today we are including criteria that will channel funds towards projects that will make a sustaining contribution to the Canadian economy and will be consistent with our national objectives and priorities.
The third principle reflected in these measures is recognition of the need to have the particular mix of employment measures tailored to regional needs. By this I refer not only to employment disparities or the fact that there are shortages of skilled workers in certain industries and regions, but also to the differing capabilities of regions to cope with problems in their respective labour markets. I have already begun consultations with my provincial counterparts to identify each region's needs, and these consultations are being carried out on an ongoing basis by our respective officials.
With these principles in mind, I am announcing the following programs relating to job creation and training:
First, we are introducing four specific job creation programs to meet special employment needs. The first is Canada community development projects. A major new program is being implemented to further national and regional priorities in such areas as fisheries enhancement, energy conservation, tourism development, and community restoration. In addition to providing valuable work, this program will contribute to the development of an expanded employment base. More than $100 million will be committed across Canada to such projects this winter and next year, with special emphasis in areas of high unemployment. This program also gives us the flexibility to respond to emerging employment problems caused by industrial dislocation, or major emergencies such as the fires and drought in western Canada.
Second, we are introducing a new technology employment program. This program is designed to assist men and women trained in technical and scientific areas to make full use of their skills in support of research and development. Funded at $7 million in the year 1980-81, this program will provide subsidies to firms and non-profit institutions that hire unemployed or under-employed post-secondary graduates to work in
research and development activities. This will help to promote innovations in manufacturing and the application of conservation and alternative energy techniques and programs across Canada.
Further, we will have a program called local economic development assistance. While the Canada community development projects are short term, it is our intention to increase the capacity of communities to meet long-term employment objectives. We will, as appropriate, use these funds for long-term employment development, through this new experimental program, as well as use existing programs such as LEAP.
The LEDA program is a new initiative aimed at providing selected communities with the means to develop comprehensive employment development strategies through non-profit community corporations established in each of these communities. LEDA will accelerate the process of economic development in these communities, first by us applying front-end money to develop appraisals, marketing and forecasts, and then provide short-term investments for equity investments in new businesses and small businesses. This is particularly appropriate for small towns and communities that want to establish a new economic base.
Funded at $3 million in 1980-81, it is intended as an experimental program and as a complement to other business development programs. Our target is to have a number of these pilot projects across Canada started in the summer and fall of this year.
Fourth, we have a community services program. This is a new program which will enable the federal government to enter into new partnership arrangements with non-profit voluntary agencies. The program will provide jobs for unemployed men and women and will, at the same time, increase, improve, and make innovations in urgently needed social and cultural services.
A major innovation of the community services program is that funding will be provided for up to three years on a diminishing share basis. Ongoing service activities will be funded, as demonstration projects, only if there is a reasonable expectation that the organizations will, over three years, be able to make other provisions for the costs of services. 1 expect that many service organizations will wish to use the program to help expand their volunteer base, or to develop fee for service operations, or simply to carry out three-year projects of real value to the community.
The labour market contains many striking and frequently unfair imbalances. In some parts of the country today, and particularly in the resource-rich areas of western Canada, industries have problems finding enough skilled workers in a growing number of occupations, while elsewhere the level of unemployment remains at intolerable levels. The economic potential of our physical resources cannot be fully achieved until we realize the human potential of the Canadian work force and, in particular, of native people and women.
June 2, 1980

Madam Speaker, in order to begin the process of establishing a balance between labour supply and demand, and to ensure that all Canadians get a fair share of the economic and social benefits of our society, we are taking the following measures.
First, we intend to add an additional $10 million to the amount available for the existing critical trades, skills, and training program. The level of funding will be increased immediately from $20 million to $30 million, an amount constrained only by the capacity of industry to utilize effectively the additional funds during the next 12 months. I am prepared to consider increasing funds for this program still further in subsequent years if industry is prepared to offer the necessary training.
We also intend to provide a special training program for native people. A special allocation of $10 million will be provided for additional training of men and women of native ancestry. The program is designed to enable them to take advantage of employment generated by new resource developments and to move into job opportunities in our urban centres.
We intend to embark on an experimental program called women in non-traditional trades. In order to help open the way for women to enter occupations traditionally dominated by men, $2 million will be provided to cover a wage subsidy of 75 per cent under the Canada Manpower Industrial Training Program to employers who train women in non-traditional occupations. This is a start-up program and, if it proves successful, it will be substantially enhanced in the following year.
Finally, because of the large number of Indo-Chinese refugees who have come to Canada, an additional $7 million will be provided for language training for refugees. This will speed the successful integration of these people into the Canadian labour market.
These initiatives, which provide a good indication of future directions in developing employment opportunities, bring total federal expenditures on training, including income support, to $834 million in 1980-81. A growing share of that training is being provided by industry, on the job site and in the skills that we so badly need.
I should also mention that another program dealing with people who have severe employment disadvantages will be presented at a later date, probably by way of legislation.
1 would like to indicate, however, that the proposed program will provide additional help to the same groups of people who will benefit from the measures I announced today as well as to other hard-to-place workers such as former prisoners and individuals with little or no education and those with physical handicaps and learning disabilities. The program will offer incentives so that disadvantaged workers are employed in the private sector. 1 have reserved $15 million in my budget for that program, one which will be later presented to Parliament.
Madam Speaker, in my capacity as minister responsible for the status of women, I would like to stress that our efforts today are only the first steps of a thorough approach to the
Employment Strategy
problems of women in the labour force. I will soon announce ongoing measures to improve employment opportunities for women, with particular priority to improving the affirmative action program in the public service.
The employment development measures outlined today will themselves have a considerable impact on the employment of women. Community services projects will assist organizations to provide services, such as day care and after-four programs, which are important to many working women and men. The cash incentive for firms to train women in non-traditional jobs is a significant innovation in terms of public policy, in Canada and in the industrial world.
Youth will also significantly benefit from the employment development measures announced today. Both the community services projects and the community development projects will serve to provide young men and women with valuable first-job experience. For young people who are qualified in technical areas, the new technology employment program offers opportunities to use their skills to advance the development and application of new technology. Young men and women under 25 can be expected to make up nearly two-thirds of the participants in our employment programs and training program expansions.
The increases in badly needed training and the new employment programs will cost $137 million in this fiscal year. These programs will be paid for with funds previously intended for tax credits and other funds set aside for programs planned by the previous government.
The measures that I outlined today are in addition to programs already planned for or in operation this fiscal year, such as the extension of the employment tax credit program. I hope members of the opposition will provide us with the co-operation which would facilitate the extension of that program so that both these announcements can go forward at the same time.

speechtext:
The hon. member will have it on his agenda sooner than he expects. Furthermore, this program must be seen in the context of additional programs such as the Summer Youth Employment program, the carry-over of Canada Works and the Local Employment Assistance Program.
In summary, these training and employment measures that I have announced are not the entire solution to our labour market problems. But they are an important beginning. We will focus on the training and employment needs of natives, women, young people, and other groups facing special difficulties in finding and retaining jobs. We will provide extra jobs in areas of high unemployment. We will reorient employment programs to serve key national and regional priorities. These measures represent the start of a new long-term approach to employment generation and national development. They point us in the right direction.
In my opening remarks I referred to the need to use our programs to meet Canada's different regional problems. There

June 2, 1980
Employment Strategy
is no group with a better understanding of such conditions than members of Parliament. In our Summer Youth Employment program, the advice and participation of members of this House have added considerably to the success of the program. It is our intention to draw on the intimate knowledge that members of Parliament have of their local areas, particularly for the locally-based Community Development Projects and through the use of local advisory groups which will assist in each constituency in the determination of priorities.
I look forward as well, Madam Speaker, to the results of the Parliamentary Task Force on Critical Skills for the Eighties, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand). This special committee will provide members of Parliament with an additional opportunity to be involved in the formulation of an employment strategy for the decade we are entering.
Within Employment and Immigration Canada, a special high level task force is being formed to examine the entire spectrum of labour market needs, including training, employment programs, employment services, mobility of workers, and industrial dislocation. I am confident that these special bodies will be productive in their work, and enable Canada to move closer to its potential in the 1980s.
Madam Speaker, may I conclude by reminding this House that these programs represent an important investment in our most priceless asset-individual Canadians. Our free market system, for all its strengths, does not always distribute opportunities equally to our people. We are all diminished when any of our fellow citizens, for whatever reason, do not have the opportunity to develop their talents to full potential and contribute their full energy to the common good.
These programs are not public charity or government bounty. They are an investment which will bear returns beyond those we now devote to resource industries, the manufacturing sector or financial enterprises. They are an investment in our fellow Canadians-our true, genuine undiminished capital for the future.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) for providing me with a copy of his statement, his press release, and a background paper. 1 received this material at noon and have taken the opportunity to read it over and reflect on it before making my response.
I must begin by expressing on behalf of the Conservative party a sense of disappointment, having waited so long for an employment strategy, to find so little that is new, exciting or helpful to Canadians. It is a small program, and the degree to which it tackles the long-term unemployment problems of this country is practically zero.
I point out to the House, for instance, that a one-cent tax on a gallon of gasoline would produce twice as much money for
employment creation as the minister has brought forward today. Public policy is always a matter of choice, and the failure of hon. members opposite to take responsible steps such as those the Conservative government was prepared to take in its budget, has strapped them for funds. Many useful social purposes must be overlooked or a band-aid must be put on them because we have a government which will not raise the money that the people of Canada require it to spend.
Unemployment is caused by bad economic decisions. The kind of unemployment which we in Canada experience today is a consequence of many bad economic decisions taken over a long period of time. Those problems affect regions in a broader sense. They affect provinces, and they affect areas within provinces. Quite frankly, 1 was looking forward today to a series of measures which would get us to the heart of the problems experienced in those parts of this country more than in other parts of this country, and as I look through the documents presented to me by the minister, I cannot find that mentality. 1 find many words asserting it to be true, but as I look at the detailed specifics of the program, I cannot find it.
In April the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) raised taxes and virtually ignored the measures in the Crosbie budget of December which would have created more employment in this country. This morning I glanced over that mini budget, and the minister left out eight specific employment creation measures related to the private sector. He chose not to reintroduce them, and we are facing a rather tragic unemployment situation in this country in the future.
How many people will we find in this country who would like to work, who would like to make a contribution to the well-being of this country, but who simply cannot find jobs? I have done a little calculating based on the figures which the government has provided to this House in the last two months, but 1 think there is general agreement among econometric forecasters that some time in the next two years the measured rate of unemployment in this country will be in the neighbourhood of 9 per cent. We are looking at measured unemployment of something in the neighbourhood of 1,100,000 Canadians. Econometricians will also tell us that as we get an increasing unemployment rate of that kind, then our hidden unemployment rate goes up.
The hidden unemployed are those people who have looked for work for so long that they are discouraged and are no longer looking for work. The best estimate of the number of people in that category at this time is 300,000 people. Then we look at this package of so-called job-creation measures which the minister has laid before the House today. With that package he says he will create something in the neighbourhood of 192,000 jobs in the current fiscal year. That is close to 200,000, and if the minister is correct and those people are working, they will not show up in this 9 per cent. When we add those three numbers, the predicted 9 per cent measured unemployment rate, the hidden unemployed, and those who are sort of tucked away in these subsidized jobs, we come to 1,600,000 Canadians who would like jobs in the real economy but cannot find them because of the economic policies of the government
June 2, 1980

opposite. That is close to 15 per cent of adult Canadians who would like to make a contribution, and 1 think that is a crime, a scandal, and something we should not continue to overlook.
1 think there are other choices available to the government opposite. Perhaps they are not available to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, but certainly they are to the government.
I would feel much more confortable as a member of this House trying to do my best to act on behalf of the Canadian people if I could see policies coming from the other side of the House which would contribute to the long-range development of this country, such as energy policies which would produce substitution, reopen coal mines in Nova Scotia, and develop the tar sands rather than retard development of the tar sands. When a tar sands plant is built, it takes $7 billion worth of wages and materials to build that mining operation, but at the same time a community must be created out of the bush which will house and service some 20,000 to 25,000 Canadians. In projects of that kind there are real jobs for those who make door knobs, doors, and steps and for those who build the houses and the plants.
I think if we trace back to the beginning of our confederation we will find that in times of trouble it was the job of the federal government to develop the economy on behalf of the people in the provinces, and it is that job which I think has been overlooked in the last decade. Our money should not be going into band-aids. Our money and our efforts should be going toward projects of real and lasting value to this nation.
Seventy thousand homes were supposed to be built in Canada this year, but they will not be built. Seventy thousand homes would create 100,000 jobs and leave 70,000 more housing units when those jobs are over. Some kind of subsidy program, in the face of high interest rates, would have produced those additional 70,000 homes, and in that way 1 think the money might have been better spent.
The program which was announced today is really an exercise in public relations which will not bear close scrutiny and examination. It is full of sympathetic words for the unemployed, but when we look at it closely we see that it reveals a tremendous number of basic inconsistencies. I do not know if that is a problem generated by the minister or a problem generated by his officials, but I would like to go into some of those inconsistencies arising out of the information which was presented to me today.
I think we need to look at the mathematics. First, the local economic development assistance program is going to cost $3 million of that $137 million, and in the minister's own background paper the number of jobs created by the expenditure of $3 million in that category is zero, so we are spending $3 million to create no jobs. In the question period the minister might care to bring us up to date on that.
I asked a question of the minister in the House of Commons a couple of weeks ago about which kinds of philosophy he might favour in the development of this program. The need for that kind of information becomes apparent when we look at
Employment Strategy
the figures provided to us by the minister. In the community services area, if we transpose the figures presented by the minister, the cost to the public treasury for each job created on a 12-month basis would be $22,000. In the new technology area, which is really the only innovation, the cost to the public treasury will be $20,000. Those are the two highest priced job-creation measures: $22,000 a year for one job, or $20,000 in the case of new technology. The lowest cost job-creation measure, according to the minister's own figures, is the employment tax credit. The minister estimates a total cost of $900 to the public treasury for one job created. There is a difference of something in the order of 25 to 1 in terms of the cost of creating new jobs on the one hand with employment tax credits and, on the other hand, with direct job-creation measures.
What about the cost of training? There is quite a bit of information in here about the fact that $834 million will be spent on training. Of that amount, $22 million is an increase; that is a 2.5 per cent increase over the money already allocated by Parliament in the main estimates. It is certainly not a significant amount. There are many, many other examples of flimflam.
I understand that you would like me to wind down as quickly as I can, Madam Speaker, but let me say that we do not have a definition of what a job is. The minister talks about 192,000 jobs. Are those one week jobs, one day jobs, or 12-month jobs? He talks about creating employment in nontraditional training for women and says he will provide 75 per cent of the wage costs for that activity. I would point out that existing programs provide 60 per cent, and in fact if you are handicapped severely they provide 85 per cent. So the program he announced here today is either a little bit of an improvement or a decline from what is available.
There is not really much change in what the minister proposes. He identified 11 programs in his background paper. One of those programs is to create employment for 1,000 people. Only one program is new, the others are a rehash of existing expenditure patterns and existing programs.
When the minister spoke about community development projects he mentioned fisheries, energy conservation, tourism, community restoration, and he went on to say that it might help us fight fire and drought in the west. Surely those are activities normal and natural to governments at both the federal and provincial levels. Are these really job-creation projects, or is this the borrowing of money from other departments to flimflam the Canadian public into believing that there is some kind of clear and consistent job-creation effort coming out of the Department of Employment and Immigration?
The minister spoke about community service program jobs which will be paid for on a declining basis: 100 per cent the first, 66 per cent the second year, 33 per cent the third year and no cost in the fourth. I ask the minister if there is any intention on the part of the Minister of Finance to provide

June 2, 1980
Employment Strategy
through the tax system better tax breaks for those who donate money to the private sector social welfare organizations. How can government start something without providing an opportunity for people in a local community to continue to make it grow and develop?
The minister bragged about the fact that in his estimates, without clearcut policy directives, 40 per cent of the jobs in training will go to women. Madam Speaker, around 45 per cent of unemployed people in Canada today are women. This program provides a disproportionate number of jobs to men. If the minister were really doing something to deal with the imbalance, we would find that 50 per cent or 60 per cent of the jobs were going to women. What he is doing is to perpetuate and intensify the disparity which already exists.
In summary, and in the questions which I hope we will be able to ask the minister subsequently, let me come back to the really basic issue, which is: is employment in Canada more likely to be the consequence of a fiscal policy? Are we, as taxpayers, better served when we provide subsidies to the private sector, or are we best served by direct employment-creation programs? I should like to engage in that debate in the context of Bill C-19 when it comes back on our plate. But I think it is impossible to proceed in a coherent fashion without clear answers on the differential costs and benefits from those three mechanisms.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to thank the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) for providing me with a copy of his statement earlier today.
To say that the measures being proposed by the minister are disappointing would be to make the understatement of the year. With rare exception, Canada has had the highest number of unemployed workers of the seven major countries in the last ten years. As of April of this year there are officially 937,000 Canadians out of work, or 8.3 per cent of the work force. When the hidden unemployed are taken into account, that figure jumps to an estimated 1,462,000 unemployed Canadians, or 12.4 per cent of the work force.
Unemployment in Canada is a national disgrace, and in the face of that all the government is capable of doing is to bring in programs that are largely cosmetic in their treatment of the most serious problem facing Canada today.
Several weeks ago 1 had the opportunity to speak in this House on the bill brought forward by the minister to extend the provisions of the Employment Tax Credit Act. At that time 1 expressed the hope that this government was finally serious about bringing forward measures which would get our country back to work. However, I also said that the record of this government was such that I was not convinced we would see the kind of action required to get the job done. Now that I saw the statement made by the minister today which alleges to deal with "employment development in the 1980s", I am convinced that this government is not serious about our unemployment crisis, or is incapable of coping with it. Rather than bringing in programs to stimulate our economy and providing
proposals for long-term job-creation, the Minister of Employment and Immigration is continuing to attack unemployment as if he were Canada's own Don Quixote, and he is doing about as much good.
Of the 14 programs to which the minister has addressed himself in the background papers which accompanied the statement, no less than eight have been in existence for some period of time, and the six new ones merely serve to indicate that the government recognizes there are problem areas within the larger problem of unemployment. These are all short-term and moderate cost programs.
There is not even a mention in this statement of the Liberal party's promise during the election campaign to develop an industrial strategy in Canada. There is no mention of the government's intention to regain control of our economy, either in the short or the long term. In fact there is nothing in this statement which will give Canadians assurances that this government is going to do much of anything to create meaningful long-term employment.
Placing an emphasis on skilled training, as these programs do, without referring to long-term job creation, simply means that somewhere down the road we will end up with an awful lot of unemployed skilled workers. Perhaps from the government's point of view it is preferable to be skilled and unemployed as opposed to being unskilled and unemployed, but this is not a view that our party shares. Rather than these measures providing solutions to unemployment, they tend to raise more questions than they provide answers.
Taking a look at the programs themselves, under the new technology employment program ail 1 can see is that it provides band-aid measures, given that 660 jobs are to be created in 1980-81 and that there are some 2,500 Ph.D.s graduating each year. Under the critical trades skills training program, the government has allocated $30 million which, in my view, is a drop in the bucket when one considers the critical trade skill shortage in Canada. Predetermined labour short trade occupations beg the question: how does the minister define or determine what those are? Under the non-traditional training for women training programs, 1 should point out to the minister that there are around 393,000 women who are unemployed, and the minister is allocating $2 million to assist these women to enter non-traditional training. At the very least the minister should be embarrassed even to introduce this kind of program to this House for our consideration.
Under the native opportunities training program, again there is not enough money in view of the decision to let the Canada Works program continue as it is now. Canada Works excludes provinces like Manitoba and Saskatchewan where there are pockets of native unemployment ranging from 50 per cent to 90 per cent. Also the focus on major resource areas presents a problem as to what happens when the resource projects are completed, that is, skilled natives versus unskilled natives. Under the community development program, this is intended to work along the same line as Canada Works and
June 2, 1980

LIP, with the exception of projects to be selected further to establish national and regional priorities.
The short-term results are that there will still be unemployment after the project is completed and there is not much money allocated to those programs. As 1 suggested, these programs raise more questions than they provide answers. If this government were serious about job creation, either in the short term or in the long term, it would have taken concrete action and accepted responsibility for the social and economic inequities being perpetrated on the Canadian population.
We need more than token gestures. We need to grasp firmly and control our abundant resource benefits. We need greater corporate financial responsibility in Canada. We need the creation of jobs and consequent reduction in unemployment, which should be one of the first priorities of this Parliament. A well-planned program of social reform must be initiated so that poverty can be completely eliminated. Low income and elderly people should be given a shelter allowance, bread and milk subsidies, and a tailor-made consumer price index should be brought down so that we can accurately assess their purchasing patterns.
A cost of living tax credit would help to alleviate the crush created by the drop in real purchasing power of family income. Inequities in income distribution should be attacked by the forms in the income tax, substituting refundable tax credits for some items which are tax deductible. We need to recognize and work toward a common goal, a guaranteed minimum income which would ensure that all members of our society receive a basic share of resources, goods and services as a part of their birthright. If this government were serious about doing something finally about the unemployment crisis in this country today, a crisis which was brought on by this administration over the last 11-year period, those are the kinds of things this government would do, instead of bringing in cosmetic items such as are contained in the program presented today which do nothing but help to cement the cynical attitude that the Canadian people have of this government and which certainly 1, as a member of this Parliament, share with them.

speechtext: 1 will start with the simple question. In terms of his background paper, could the minister define what a job is?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, considering that the hon. member at one time was reputed to be an academic of some note in the definition of work, it strikes me as seemingly odd
Employment Strategy
he would ask a question which he has already defined for himself. It is someone who is gainfully employed.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Could the minister indicate, whether my interpretation is correct-if somebody is employed on a project for one day or a half day, then that person is presumed to have been given a job by the public? Is that the kind of number we are dealing with in the minister's background paper?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member is deliberately trying to confuse the issue. What we are talking about is that when we put these programs forward, the different organizations such as voluntary organizations, municipalities and others, make applications for projects which we will measure according to their meaningful value. Obviously a job that will last one day would have very little chance of being considered, certainly when one takes into account that we will be asking for assessment and measurement by members of Parliament who we know are always very discerning in their judgment and attitude.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Dealing with the 192,000 jobs the minister is asserting he is creating, if we were to use a different definition of 52 weeks of work, then we might be dealing with the public sector creating something like 30,000 or 40,000 jobs. Does the minister have an estimate of the more normal meaning of the word "job" where they last for a fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is nothing that requires us to define a job as lasting a year. A job is when one is making an income for the work one is doing. We have estimated in the extension of the programs we have announced today, combined with those that will be brought about as a consequence of the employment tax credit, that we will be creating opportunities for well over 80,000 participants, whether they last nine months or a year. In some cases they will last beyond a year because we have said very clearly in these programs that under the community development projects, the community services program and others, they can last a year, 18 months, or three years. So, what we might lose on the nine-month end of it, we will pick up on the other end of it.
I do not want to tell the member something I assume he knows from his own background, but 1 think in any labour force people are constantly changing jobs and coming in and out of the work force. However, we are defining a series of work opportunities and training opportunities that are well defined by the sponsors of these or by the agencies that put them forward which would provide work particularly in those areas where work is most needed in the high unemployment areas that sometimes may last nine months or 15 months. We will be measuring and assessing those projects on their merits.

June 2, 1980
Employment Strategy

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I note with interest that the minister is now restricted by the envelope system in the amount of funds he can use. In the opening paragraphs he mentioned that the aim of this program is for fishing enhancement. I should like to ask the minister how much money was taken from the salmon enhancement program and applied to this program for the fishing enhancement part of it?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to make one small correction in the statement of the hon. member. We were not limited so much by the envelope system but by the niggardly estimates that were put in by the previous government for job creation. That is what we were limited by.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
One thing which gave me frustration when 1 took on this portfolio was to realize the previous government had totally wiped out all the direct job-creation programs, so that applying employment opportunities in those areas where they were most severely needed, or to the groups that most needed it, was not possible because they were going to employ exclusively the tax credit system. According to my figures, for example, some 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the job credit programs do not go into the high unemployment areas. So, what we were basically limited in is the very poor judgment and poor choice of the previous government. We have attempted in our best efforts to try to improve that in the time we have had. If we had not done this now, there would have been a total vacuum in job creation in this country for the next six months and thereby there would have been very major problems created.
But I can assure the hon. member that we did not take any money from his salmon enhancement program. 1 have discussed with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) that if a department such as his wished to put up capital works or capital money of that kind, then we would add to it the employment money so that major fish enhancement programs could take place. I think that is something which would be determined and blueprinted in each local region. We will be establishing a very strong area of autonomy for each of our regional officers to consult with the provinces and the private sector in each of the provinces to tailormake a jobtraining program which best suits their area. In those cases other federal departments could come in and add capital moneys to provide for a supplement so that we can undertake larger projects.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
1 am glad 1 had such a short question. Since the minister says he is taking nothing from the salmon enhancement program for the fisheries enhancement, 1 will be looking to the future to see whether the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) will be discussing the amount he is spending on the salmon enhancement program and allowing the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to make up for his shortfall.
I should like to ask the minister about what 1 believe is called the new critical trades training program, or an appellation such as that. That is a good bureaucratic word; in street language it is called an apprenticeship training program. Could I have a short answer to that?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in each of the provinces there are a number of ways the provincial governments organize the training of skilled workers. What we attempt to provide through our critical skills program is ways of paying allowances and ways of helping them pay for those programs. In some cases it is applied to apprenticeship programs; in other cases it is applied directly to the employer to provide on-the-job training on the factory site. It has flexibility in its application. That is why we do not try to restrict it to one use or the other.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in his statement the minister said he wants to aid target groups, and specifically he talked about the critical skill shortage in Canada. I have had some considerable experience in that particular area through the community college structure in Ontario. As a result of that experience 1 know personally that most employers have extreme difficulty in identifying the groups that the minister is attempting to identify. Could the minister advise the House what procedures or mechanisms he plans to use to do the kind of thing that employers seem incapable of doing?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not share the low regard for employers that the hon. member has. For the last two or three months 1 have been meeting with a variety of employment groups, both in the trade unions and in the products sector, and we have discussed the variety of skill shortages that they encounter. They know very well exactly what kinds of shortages they have. You only have to go onto the shop floor to know who they cannot employ. If it is a problem for those associated with the community colleges to identify that need, maybe that is one reason why we have difficulty, that those in the operation of educational institutions have not been communicating well enough with those actually working on the shop floor to identify what those needs are.
I can assure the hon. member that with the means we have available we put together a major catalogue of those areas where there are shortages, and we are attempting to work with each of the employment occupational groups. I would suggest to the hon. member that if he wants a good overview he should go back to the reports prepared by the previous Liberal government when they established the sector-by-sector approach, under the minister of state for economic development, which established a series of categories of skill needs in this country. I think that has proven to be very accurate forecasting.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can assure the hon. minister that I have a regard for employers about equal to his own. My comments were based on personal experience with them. The minister identified social services such as day care, crisis
June 2, 1980

centres, and home care for the elderly, as essential services several years ago, or his ministry did. Would the minister tell the House whether the federal government has a commitment to see that these programs are not just implemented but are guaranteed to be ongoing? Are there any guarantees that after the programs have been completed they are not going to be left in the lurch and that there will be some federal moneys available, or will they be into short-term programs? What does the minister plan to do to make sure that those programs will be ongoing and will prove to be worth while? Could the minister give us some information in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 will be very pleased to answer the hon. member's question as I think it is an important one. We were approached by a number of organizations, particularly those representing women, which indicated that one of the real problems in developing proper opportunities for employment of women in this country was a lack of support services such as child care, lunch and after-school programs, and various other forms of support services in the community. What had happened in the last two or three years, because of a kind of neo-Conservative philosophy bandied about or displayed by too many provincial governments and municipal governments, was that those services were the first to be cut and were in short supply. We feel that through this kind of program we will be able to assist such groups to regenerate those kinds of programs. We made it very clear to them that we could not usurp the jurisdictional responsibility of provinces for ongoing services.
This program is designed to provide an extra boost for groups and organizations in the non-profit, volunteer sector to start new programs which would help them to strengthen their organizations. For example, if a group or organization in the child care field wanted to develop a new volunteer base for its program, or fund raising for its program, this program is designed to do that. As we pointed out in our statement, we have extended it over a three-year period. We would measure and judge the program on grounds which would either indicate it would terminate after those three years or provide ongoing support beyond that.
We are doing it on a trial basis to see if it will work. What we think is critical is that we provide employment opportunities in that field and at the same time provide the service that will enable other people to become employed.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Past experience has shown. Madam Speaker, that once those programs have run their course and have proved to be useful to the community and the groups they were designed to assist, the funding has dried up, even though the need continues. The groups have been spending around 90 per cent of the staffs time and energy on fund-raising activities and the other volunteer services have been getting about 10 per cent.
Has the minister any specific plan to provide that once the funding has terminated this undesirable situation will not occur again, that there will be continued funding where these
Employment Strategy
programs have proven successful to the community and the user groups?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I can explain it to the hon. member this way, that the ongoing support for the social services communities must come basically from the provinces. As he well knows, at the present moment the federal government pays 50 per cent of most of the costs of CAP. Those programs will be renegotiated and discussed with the provinces as the agreements are put in place. We are not trying to displace that major, ongoing social service funding arrangement between the provinces and the federal government with this program.
What we are trying to provide are supplementary programs to enable community non-profit groups to engage in extra activities that they would not otherwise be able to afford. For example, some people I spoke to this weekend who are in the child care field said their workers are so busy trying to provide the basic services that they do not have time to extend any additional services in the community, to measure needs, to do fund raising, to strengthen their base, or to develop the parental, volunteer side of their organization. Under this kind of program they would have the means to strengthen their organization under well-defined program objectives.
We are not only attempting to provide employment opportunities, particularly for women who will be working in this field. These are the areas that were cut out by the previous government through Canada Works programs and by municipal and provincial governments. It will enable those existing organizations to provide for extra activities, and demonstration projects or innovative projects that they could test themselves, or to provide supplementary activity. That is the reason we are putting this program into effect-to provide employment and to help those organizations strengthen their activity.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have two questions, but 1 shall ask both at the same time. If the minister considers the over-all economic conditions in the country he will surely realize that in the auto industry, the farm implement industry, the housing industry, the steel industry, the retailing industry in general, the construction industry in general, and in the mining industry, there are massive employment cutbacks. Many people are being laid off in all those industries. Keeping that in mind, looking at the programs which the minister has brought in, and if we were in a period of full employment with many employment opportunities, and since this matter deals with a peripheral unemployment group, then I would say that this program is not bad.
Keeping in mind that we face massive unemployment and that we are following the economy of the United States into a further downturn, can the minister tell us exactly what programs such as these will do for people who are now becoming unemployed and who face the prospect of long-term unemployment because their jobs are disappearing due to the major downturn of the economies of the North American continent?

June 2, 1980
Employment Strategy
Can the minister specifically address himself to the matter of women in non-traditional trades where allowing $2 million to the extent of funding to 75 per cent of the total cost means 280 jobs at $10,000 a year per person. What in heaven's name is this supposed to do for unemployment?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: 1 am glad that the hon. member decided to ask his two questions at once. I would ask the hon. member not to make a speech and be brief in his questions. We do not wish to spend too much time on this matter, although I know that there are other hon. members who wish to ask questions of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 think that the hon. member asked four questions and made five statements, not just two questions. However, the hon. member asked a very legitimate question. I am sure that everyone in this House would agree that major changes are taking place in the economic and industrial structure of North America. The problem will not be solved in a matter of two or three months.
As 1 said in my statement, this is why we have introduced a parliamentary committee, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), so that all members may join in public consultation over the next two months or three months with all the people in the country who are affected, to make their representations and concerns known. At the same time 1 have established within my department a major task force staffed by people from throughout the public service to begin working at the long-term public requirements in Canada in the 1980s. This task force will be chaired by the deputy minister.
As a result of those two major initiatives, 1 hope to be able to come to this House by the end of next year, in either October, November or December, with a major paper which will outline the employment requirements, what the public sector should be doing and what the private sector should be doing. This paper will also give an indication of our future direction based on those two initiatives. I agree with the hon. member that we must take a look at these matters.
In the meantime, the hon. member should not judge these particular programs as the government's only answer. As I said in my statement, the government is spending over $800 million this year in training programs. What I did was that I put more money into that fund. Over 250,000 people are being trained at the moment in this country with the support of the government. It seems that the hon. members ignore this obvious fact, that the government has a number of initiatives already in place.
What the government has tried to do with this program is to add to and supplement the other programs to fill in some of the vacuum areas, mainly in the area of direct job-creation programs. The government is fully aware of and sensitive to the needs, and it is trying to respond. As a responsible government should do, it is consulting first with those who are affected, looking at and reviewing its own programs, and, in the six fiscal months remaining in this year, it is using all the
available resources to apply to the hardest core problems, the special target needs in our society.
We must remember that what this program is doing is not with regard to a full year's financing. The cabinet was formed on March 4. There are only six months remaining in this fiscal year, and those are the months in which the $137 million will be applied. We cannot measure, as did the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), on the basis of a full year. What we are trying to do is correct the mistakes of the Conservative government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Order. I have a list of the hon. members who have risen. I will allow only one question each. The list includes the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley), the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Kushner), the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), and the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). The hon. members may not be called in that order to ask their questions. I would ask all hon. members to state their questions carefully and briefly. Each questioner will be allowed only one question, otherwise we will be here until five o'clock.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a point of order. 1 have been on my feet from the beginning, and 1 did not hear my riding called out as one on the list. 1 hope that you will include me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: That is true. The hon. member is on the list. There is another piece of paper here.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a few very specific questions for the minister.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: One question.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: It is one question, and 1 will get on with it. 1 believe that the minister mentioned in his statement that constituency advisory groups will be reintroduced. I would like to know whether those constituency advisory groups which, by the way, were abolished by the previous government last year, when it did away with the entire Canada Works program for the west end of Montreal, will apply to all the community programs, will the money be allocated on a constituency basis, and will there be a minimum amount of money for each constituency, which was not the case under the Conservative program.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his very pertinent question. I would like to answer yes to all three of his questions: Yes, the money will be allocated right across Canada, one region will not be selected over another, and there will be a basic constituency allocation for every constituency. There will be factors built in with regard to those areas of high unemployment, and those areas which have special needs such as native organizations will get a larger amount for distribution. Each constituency will have a basic
June 2, 1980

amount for its community development program. The constituency advisory groups that we established are being designed to enable a full and accurate reading of the real priorities in those areas. This reading will be provided through the person who is perhaps in the best position to judge, the member of Parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister in his statement indicated that while governments can move in these areas, there is a limit to what they can do, and that government efforts by themselves are not sufficient. What is required is a sound economic program to involve the private sector in job creation, co-operation between the provinces, and a whole host of other requirements. 1 am sure that one of the things which the minister would have in mind to assist what he has indicated is only a stop-gap measure to augment a program that is in existence now, would be some basis upon which he and we, as members of Parliament, and the public that we represent could understand the economic plan and economic direction of the government.
The minister must be as confused as everyone else with regard to the statements made by the deputy minister of finance in the Senate the other day and the statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in the House about whether we will allow the deficit to grow or to decrease.
It is a confusing situation not only to employers but to everyone else.
Would the minister, given the importance of a sound base upon which any employment program can be built, call upon the Minister of Finance to end the uncertainty by bringing forth a plan of action and a budget so that the minister and other ministers will finally have some sense of direction as to where this country will go, and so that there can be real fight against unemployment in this country?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would want to say to the hon. member that it depends on which side of the House one is on as to how one hears things. I am most impressed by the clarity and logic of the Minister of Finance in presenting the economic position of this government. By comparison to the statement made by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), when he predicted in his budget speech last December, that an additional 200,000 people in the country would be employed, the statements made by the Minister of Finance are exemplary.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question will take some leading into, but 1 will be brief. The minister has indicated to the House that he has done nothing but shuffle old money into new programs. He seems to ignore the fact that the government is borrowing $3 billion more than the Conservative government intended to borrow, which suggests that the minister has lost the fight for more money for more programs. That is the first point, and it is indicative.
My second point before I lead into the question is that the government in its previous incarnation as a government promised the Canadian people support for urban transit. It boot-
Employment Strategy
legged that in later on top of the program which was used to help solve the problem of railways at overcrossings, and called it the urban transit program. Today the minister indicated, after releasing the press release, that the major component of the program, the $100 million-which he indicates is no more money to be redistributed than there was in the beginning- will also be used for industrial relocation relief and for help in drought situations.
Is the minister, in fact, not saying to this House that he has lost the fight for more money for job creation? Second, has he already had to concede that some of those funds should be stripped from job creation for local salvation problems where they exist and are in real need, that those funds are going to be stripped from job creation programs so that in fact under this program we are going to wind up with substantially less money in direct job creation than would have been true?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 find that a very surprising question. When 1 became the minister of this department there was no money for direct job creation. The Tories had stripped the funds totally from the estimates. There was not a cent left for direct job creation.
What we have tried to do is to restore the concept of direct job creation so that we can target in on very specific areas of unemployment because there was no money left in the budget by the previous administration to do that. It had decided, I guess for philosophical reasons which I accept, that the only means of creating jobs would be through the tax credit system. What was very clear in our measurement, that while the tax credit system has utility in some areas, and has been an effective program in part, it cannot be used to target in on the special problems of women, or of natives or the problems of high unemployment areas. The tax credit system is not employed, for example, in areas where there is unemployment over 11 per cent or 12 per cent, where there is not a small business component to take advantage of it. He says shuffle the money around. It is not so easy to shuffle the money around when the money is not there to begin with. What we had to do is restore direct expenditures of the government in the job-creation field because those direct expenditures had been removed.
1 would say to the hon. member that I do not agree that calling a necessity to respond to problems of reforestation, for example, in northern forests or on the prairie regions, is just simply a make-work project. There are major economic problems in those areas. I think nothing could be more useful than for this government to assist, whether it be in Windsor or in northern Manitoba, those Canadians to get back on their feet and start recreating an economic base. That goes back to the original principle of our statement: do we want to create work that serves more useful, meaningful job opportunities and national objectives? That is what we are trying to do. We are trying to twin those two objectives so that we get more bang for the buck".

June 2, 1980
Employment Strategy

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have a question for the minister regarding the programs, particularly those directed toward women, at least that is the suggestion in the statement. There has been a good deal of rhetoric expressed in recent months concerning the role of women. Certainly in the Speech from the Throne there were some welcome initiatives that were proposed. However, I would suggest that the amount of $2 million which is allocated in this particular program is really an insult to Canadian women, and what we should be looking at is a far greater amount in direct funding rather than essentially a bribery of the corporate sector to the tune of 75 per cent of the cost of the jobs.
I ask the minister to indicate in this area, partly as the minister responsible for the status of women, now that he has finally had a chance to put his rhetoric into action, whether this is the best that he can come up with. First will he not make a commitment to this House to restore the funding to Outreach programs which was slashed by the previous Liberal government? Second, will he not make a commitment to make direct funding for child care facilities, instead of hoping that some of the other funding which he has proposed will trickle down to the child care area? One of the ways in which women can be encouraged to enter the labour market is by adequate child care being available. Will the minister ensure that there will be substantially increased funding for child care?
Third, will the minister assure us that there will be tough affirmative action taken in the public sector to lead the way in this important area, rather than just making a suggestion that $2 million, which is really a slap in the face to Canadian women, is adequate to deal with the serious problems facing women in this time of difficult unemployment for all Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is sometimes unfortunate that certain members of this House are so eager and active in trying to engage in their own rhetoric that they refuse to see the real value when certain initiatives are being taken.
1 feel that it is too bad that the hon. member would be so anxious to condemn what is basically an important issue that has been discussed with a number of womens1 organizations across this country. I would say to hon. members that, in discussing the problem with a group called women in trades, for example, the fundamental problem that they faced after they had acquired certain skills in the workplace was providing an opportunity in the private employment sector to gain access into the specific shop.
I am trying to answer the question. If the hon. member does not want to listen, then maybe we should not talk about it. But I want to answer this question as honestly as 1 can.
When we examined what we could do and discussed it with different groups, they said that it is a starter program. You cannot inject a massive new program with money without seeing if it works. We put the money in. As I said, it is only within the latter six months of this fiscal year. If it proves to be effective, as 1 said in my statement, we will substantially enhance that program as a way of ensuring that women get
that opportunity in the non-traditional fields. But first we have to test it out. That is the intention of the program, namely, to test that particular formula to see if it works. If it works, I will guarantee to the hon. member that there will be substantially more funds for that program, and for other programs. But I am not going to rush into a program and spend all kinds of money without having an idea of whether it works or not.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS TO PROVIDE JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
For the hon. member's information, at the present moment we have close to 80,000 women in training programs across Canada. By talking about 600 or 800, the hon. member does a disservice to mention those figures. There are close to over 80,000 women in training programs sponsored by the federal Government of Canada across the nation.
I can also tell the hon. member that the funds to Outreach have already been restored and we intend to increase them and develop new Outreach programs. We are consulting on that aspect at the present moment. As far as affirmative action is concerned, I would certainly tell the hon. member that we are presently working on an affirmative action program both in the private sector where we have signed a number of agreements with private sector employers, and we will be applying the same system to the public sector. We are presently negotiating to make that happen. 1 think that the hon. member will find that we will be living up exactly to the commitments made in the throne speech.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
