speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have arrived at a critical junction in our country's history. The vastness and diversity of Canada have always contributed to conflicting demands upon the federal system. Today these demands have climaxed into separatist movements in both the east and the west.
I do not pretend that this bill, the first of three which I will be introducing dealing with the question of provincial representation, will make more than a modest effort to slow down the divisive tendencies so evident in our society today. But I would like to think that these bills are in keeping with the spirit expressed both by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in the House following the referendum, when they spoke of the legitimate aspirations of all Canadians and the need for more effective and representative national institutions and mechanisms.
My bills do recognize that provinces have legitimate aspirations and moreover, valid demands for input into decision making when the outcome of those decisions is of fundamental importance to them.
As it presently stands, the act establishing the Canadian Radio-television Commission does not provide for provincial input into the appointing of commissioned membership. Changing the act to require the approval of the majority of provinces for these appointments would go a long way toward overcoming provincial accusations that the federal government is ignoring the concerns of those regions outside of central Canada. These changes would, in effect, provide a mechanism whereby the provinces could ensure that their concerns would be recognized. At the same time these amendments would ensure that the administrative efficiency of the commission would not be impaired.

As members know, the amount deals with projected budgetary and non-budgetary cash requirements tabled on April 21. I should like to begin by placing before the House examples of the way in which past Liberal governments have spent the taxpayers money. It goes without saying, I believe, that the policy of the present government, if it follows the pattern of Liberal governments in the past, will be: spend and spend, don't tax and don't tax, in an attempt to elect and elect. The examples 1 have selected are taken from a book entitled "A Legacy of Spending", published on the west coast; this is the second printing, I understand it has gone through many more since this edition was published. I bring them before the House on the premise that most Canadians will see the link between deficit spending and inflation, which is what most of us are concerned about. My first example, taken from this work, might be called item one:
Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau went on national television in a major press conference to talk to the Canadian people about inflation and the country's financial future. He said this-
There are, now, I think, only 17 members sitting opposite.
"We would be on the way to national disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control. To spend vast sums on welfare, education and other programs while allowing inflation to continue-

Finance Minister Jean Chretien introduced legislation in the Commons which would give the government authority to borrow up to $9 billion . . . the request for new borrowing authority comes on top of a $17 billion authority to borrow which the government received in March of this year.

My next item, number three, is a quotation from the Nobel Prize Winner in Economics, Milton Friedman, speaking on CBC Radio on February 20, 1977:
Borrowing Authority Act
There is only one place where inflation is made in Canada, and that is Ottawa. The unions don't make inflation for the simple reason that the unions do not own a printing press on which they can turn out those multi-coloured pieces of paper called money. The reason you have inflation is because the government has been printing too much and spending too much.
An example of this which many of us think of, though it is not in this book, is the loss of $130 million which Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, a Crown corporation, incurred selling its Candu reactor to Argentina, of all places.
The next example has to do with contracts. 1 believe members opposite know very well what contracts to their friends and consultants have amounted to over the years.
During 1975 and 1976 there were about 5,000 outside people under contract to the federal government to 72 departments, agencies or Crown corporations. The total cost to the Canadian taxpayer in those two years was some $148 million.
The latest example of what 1 call the government's use of contracts to reward its friends is that of the contract which was awarded to their candidate in Calgary West, Doug Laugh-lin, whom I know and find to be a pleasant individual. He has been hired by the Minister of Immigration and Transport at a salary, I am informed, of $50,000 a year, which is higher, I understand, than any other member of the same department.
I think the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) conceded last week that a large part of his job, if not the only part of his job, would be to try to build up the Liberal party in western Canada. I assure hon. members opposite that it will take more than Doug Laughlin or 50 or 100 Doug Laughlins at $50,000 a year to do anything about getting the Liberal party off the ground or out from under the ground in western Canada. However, I cite that as one example of why hon. members opposite are asking for $12 billion in borrowing authority.
Item number five is simply figures respecting the deficits of the Post Office. I will only give the last few because it will get monotonous if I go beyond that. In 1972-73 the deficit was $90 million. In 1973-74 it was $177 million. In 1974-75 it was $320 million. In 1975-76 it was $546 million. In 1976-77 it was $671 million. In 1977-78 it was $567 million. 1 am told that the current deficit for the Post Office is of the order of approximately $700 million.

Other unions will understandably want the same thing in terms of lunch breaks, and this will increase the deficit by about $30 million. When all the other government agencies and public employees ask for the same thing, that could amount to hundreds of millions of dollars.
Item number six deals with the question of the burden of debt. Please bear in mind that this is a couple of years old, but I do not think the situation has improved. The total direct government debt at the end 1976 was $96 billion, of which about $60 billion was owed by the federal government. I am quoting here:

Canadian governments are already deeply in debt at a time when they ought to be able to borrow to stimulate recovery. They have gone into debt to provide services and allowances the economy could not afford-to cover deficits, in fact. Governments have taken too much of the capital that was needed by private industry to build new or expanded plants-

Mr. Friedman wrote that the way a budget deficit is financed is the heart of the inflation problem. In his view, money supply changes alone account for long-term price changes. In his opinion, the only condition for prosperity without inflation is for the central bank to:
-stabilize the rate of increase in the money supply at a rate approximately equal to the real rate of growth in the economy, say 4 per cent to 5 per cent per annum.
What is not appreciated is that he is not opposed to deficits in times of unemployment, but would not allow governments to pay for them by means of new currency printed for that exclusive purpose. He says that politicians permitted to meddle with money simply print too much of it, which in turn brings inflation, destroys the frugal instincts of its citizens and in turn:
-creates conditions that force governments to play a larger role in the system. In due course, inflation leads to economic collapse, climbing unemployment, and hence an even larger role for the state.
Some hon. members will recall a few years ago when the government of Mr. Callaghan in Britain was finally converted, I think. Inflation then was running in Britain at about 25 per cent a year and unemployment, interestingly, had never been higher since the great depression. Trying to convince people that inflation and unemployment are connected is a difficult but worth-while task, in my view.
Next I should like to refer to John Kenneth Galbraith who, as we all know, was originally a Canadian and has written many books. It is interesting to note that as early as 1952 he concluded that inflation was:
-the clear and present economic danger of our times.
In "The Affluent Society", which we probably all read, Galbraith wrote that inflation:
-falls on the weakest members of society, those with fixed incomes and those too poor or powerless to bargain for compensating wage increases.
His solution, as many of us know, is price controls backed by appropriate fiscal and monetary policy.
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to conclude at five o'clock, or perhaps just before five o'clock to allow my hon. friend a question. I am proud to have been a member of this House through these several decades in which we have greatly changed the picture from what it was in the early years about which I have just talked. Instead of a pension of only $20 a month payable at age 70 with a severe means test, now we have a pension of about $186 a month payable to everyone in Canada who is age 65 or more, who meets the residence requirement, and we have the guaranteed income supplement which can be had on top of that, and also the Canada Pension Plan. I say to the government that consideration ought to be given to the propositions set out in this resolution.
The thing I feel is most needed is what is stated in the first part of the resolution, namely, the lowering of the eligible age. We have it down to 65, but the number of people, particularly women, in years just below that, from 62 to 65 or 60 to 65, or
Old Age Security
even younger for that matter, who are in dire straits, is a disgrace to the good name of Canada. The arrangements we now have for the spouse's allowance do not meet the situation at all. The spouse's allowance helps some women in that age bracket, namely, those who are married to spouses who are over 65, but it provides nothing at all for women who are single, whether they are unmarried, divorced or what have you. The plight, as we all know, of unattached older women in this country is something of which we ought to be very deeply ashamed.
I feel very strongly that the answer to that is not more programs like the spouse's allowance, not programs that have a marital test in them, not programs that have a means test in them. My contention is that the most logical and humane approach is to provide the pension at age 60 to persons who are out of the labour market. It is very simple to apply that test. We had that kind of test once on the Canada Pension Plan benefits between the ages of 65 and 70, but we removed it in favour of no test at all.
In other words, I am not advocating that pensions be universal at 60 as they are at 65, but I say that those who are out of the labour market ought to get that opportunity, ought to have the right to receive their pensions, both old age security and the Canada Pension Plan. It would not take long for that kind of program to do far more by way of providing jobs for young people than was proposed today by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). Just make it possible for persons between the age 60 and 65, by leaving the labour market, to draw old age security and the Canada Pension Plan and, 1 suggest, several hundred thousand jobs would be opened up right away.
That, however, is not my main purpose in making this proposal; the main reason I do so is that I think it just does not make sense and does not accord with the way we think about things in Canada for our older people to be suffering at all.
I suppose if this debate is not finished by six o'clock some of those who take part will say they are sympathetic with my viewpoint, that they want to do something for older people but we cannot afford it, that this is a time of restraint. That is what finance minister Charles Dunning said to J. S. Woods-worth when he first proposed a pension of $20 a month at age 70-the treasury could not afford it, the country would go broke. When the bill went to the Senate their honours opposed it because they said it would not be good for the old people to be getting pensions out of the public treasury! The pensions they were getting over there for life did not seem to bother them. It did not drive them to the dogs but it would do that to older people generally.
Let us not have that kind of statement today, Mr. Speaker. Even if it is a time of restraint it is not the time to put the burden of that restraint on the weaker members of our society. Families do not do that. If a family is in economic straits it does not put the main burden on the weakest and most helpless members of the family; it does some sharing and sees to it that

the family as a unit gets along. Let us not put the burden of our economic problems today on those who are older by condemning them to continue to live below the poverty line, while we find money to spend billions on aircraft, while we find it possible to bail out Chrysler Corporation and outfits like that, while we appoint Dr. Cliff Mclsaac and the Hon. Leon Balcer to study the possibility of raising the pay of MPs. If they do recommend that, 1 hope we will have enough decency not to go for it while senior citizens are still living below the poverty line. Do not tell me that restraint has to be borne on the backs of those least able to bear it.
The whole business of government is one of deciding where to spend the money. Sometimes in this place you would think the job of Parliament is to keep government from spending money. 1 am not against government spending money but 1 want it spent fairly. It is not being spent fairly when our senior citizens are suffering as they do today.
As I say, this applies generally, Mr. Speaker, but it applies particularly to elderly women who are unattached. These things could be resolved by accepting the proposition set out in this motion.
I say in the first part of the motion that 1 think the eligible age should be brought down to 60, and I say in the latter part of the motion that the amount of the pension ought to be increased. The figure I give is $400 per month which is a little bit more than the total of old age security and guaranteed income supplement will be after July 1. My proposal is that it be on a universal basis. 1 am still as sold as I was the day I first came here on the proposition that it is not just, decent, and humane to say to older people that to get what they need they have to prove their poverty. Tax it back from those who do not need it. We could do it if we had a sensible income tax system. We should not require people to submit to an income or means test, however. My proposal is that it be paid universally and that the few-the 8 per cent or 10 per cent at the top who do not need it-can be required to pay it back. Let us not continue this concept of a means test as it applies with respect to the guaranteed income supplement.
I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) agrees with me, but she always has to defend the other position. The other day she said she wondered why we kept pushing the concept of universality when, after all, it had been won. Then she said she suddenly got the idea that maybe the reason we do it in this corner of the House is because we are afraid that it has not been eternally won. She is dead right, Mr. Speaker. Battles do not stay won if people do nothing about them. There have been voices in this very session saying that we should reconsider the whole position and not stay with universality, that maybe we should take it away from some and give it to others. Unless some of us keep fighting for the principle of universality, we could lose even the universality we have as it applies now with respect to the basic amount of the old age pension.

When the hon. member for Victoria became the minister of veterans affairs-and I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will back me up on what I am about to say-one of the priorities of the then minister and the government was indicated in one of its earliest pieces of legislation, a bill which 1 think would be acceptable to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if it was introduced today. I hope that the government, when the questions are asked in the House of Commons with regard to the position of veterans-a group of people to whom this country owes a great obligation and its independence-whether the questions come from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre or the hon. member for Victoria, that the answer will not be that the matter is before government. This matter has been before government for some time. There is a bill ready, and it should be introduced and dealt with expeditiously. Such a bill is important, and it would have received speedy passage by our government. It is important that the bill be introduced and passed now.
While I pay tribute to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who has urged that cause, I want to pay tribute as well to the hon. member for Victoria who, being a veteran himself,

when he was minister, and knowing the plight of these people, pressed the case in cabinet and brought a bill to the House of Commons which, I wish, could have been dealt with before the government fell.
There is not a member of Parliament, no matter from whence he or she may come and regardless of the constituency which he or she represents in this House, who will not say to anyone who asks that there are people in his or her own constituency who are disadvantaged as a result of raging inflation. Elderly people are disadvantaged by the requirements of old age, being unique in themselves, and the absolute inability of the present pension system and the amounts paid under it, even with the $35 which we added to the GIS last week through the mutual consent of the House. I am sure that there is no member who is prepared to say that the present amounts are adequate. If there are such persons, then I think those members are out of touch with the system.
A week or so ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) released a study on the future of the nation's elderly. The study said that if the prognosis for the future is to be gleaned from the report, one would have to describe it as bleak, and the largest burden would appear to be falling on women who tend to live longer. I hope that the government, spurred on by this motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, will speed up consideration of the changes which must be made in the pension system.
The changes apply not only to the public area, with which we can deal directly once the study which is under way is completed, but to the private sector which also has problems that must be addressed. The big bite with the whole pension system is with respect to inflation. This report notes that only a handful of private sector pension plans offer increases to help offset the effects of inflation on employees. In many places there have been ad hoc contributions to partially offset, but according to the report, such adjustments really only go about half way to answer the effects of inflation. That report was tabled in the House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
With respect to the public sector plans which have been described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and with respect to the private sector plans, what we have is an inadequate system which cannot meet the needs of a population which is aging, not to mention the increase in the proportion of that population which is growing old. People are living longer today, and the figures in this area are quite dramatic.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that, in the name of restraint, it is inhumane and improper to look to those who are no longer in the work force, who are no longer contributing to inflation and who are, in fact, the victims of inflation to bear the burden of that restraint program. I am not suggesting that the balancing in government is easy. I was in government and I know that it is difficult. However, this is an increasing problem and that is why I am concerned.

The Globe and Mail of this morning indicated that the government is considering removing the indexation of income tax in order to reduce the government's budget deficit. Such a measure would not impact very heavily upon me or upon any other member of this House, but it will impact very heavily on people of lower incomes. Before the government moves to implement such a proposition, it must think very carefully about what it is doing. 1 believe that the index feature was put in place to help taxpayers escape the ravages of inflation. I think that that indexing feature as it applies to income tax can have a very important bearing on taxpayers of moderate income, and that includes old age pensioners.
When the government considers its programs for pensions and superannuation that are available to its own public servants, it is equally important that it not give with one hand and take away with the other, all in the name of restraint.
There has been a considerable amount of discussion over the years. It was discussed by the government of which I was a member, and it was discussed during the course of the Thirtieth Parliament. There was an attempt during the course of the thirtieth Parliament to come to some balancing of the equities in the course of that debate. 1 think that that balancing of the equities should at least be maintained. I think our efforts should be directed toward looking at the somehow private and the public system and attempting to marry them so that out of it there will come some adequate form of security for one's old age.
The most significant statement that appeared out of that report on the plight of the elderly, tabled by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, was this:
If the real value of such pensions is allowed to erode to the extent that occurred in the 1970s, the whole employer-sponsored system could well be seriously called into question.
What does that say to people who grow old, leave the work place, and have these inadequate pension plans in the private sector? They could ask about the obligations of the government in the public sector. What it says then is that we have an obligation, growing at an alarming extent, to examine the public sector side to see whether there can be an appropriate marrying. If we allow the pension systems in this country, both public and private, not to meet the needs of Canadians, and the failure to meet that need grows with the reality of the economic situation in the country, then I want to ask everyone in this House what they are going to say to old age pensioners, what they are going to say to retired people when they come and ask what the government intends to do about the situation that exists.
I guess a lot depends on one's view of the role of government. Quite frankly, I think if it is any role at all to govern, its primary role is to protect the disadvantaged. They can be disadvantaged because of physical handicaps, because they need new training to get other jobs, because social programs have changed or because they have grown old. They have become either unable to compete or are in such a position that
one ought not to ask them to compete in the work force. So those are the problems that face us as we go down the road.
The motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was a very timely one. I want to give you some indication of the seriousness of the problem that is facing the men and women of our generation and the generations that are to come who will sit in this House. 1 want to give some information that was in the study tabled by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have this opportunity to discuss this motion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I was interested in his biographical remarks made at the beginning. I believe the hon. member was born in Los Angeles. At the time he was born, my mother was living in Los Angeles, moved to Winnipeg shortly after when her father, my grandfather, became a minister of a church in Winnipeg. So we have that background in common.
This motion reflects the hon. member's ongoing interest in our public pension system. 1 consider the debate quite timely, particularly in view of the fact that we have recently debated plans to improve the retirement income system in Canada.
In my opinion, it would be most appropriate for me to focus my initial remarks on a brief discussion of these plans. In so doing, I am hopeful that at least some of the concern raised in the hon. member's motion will be alleviated.
I wish to refer specifically to two announcements made in the Speech from the Throne which give proof of this government's commitment to meet the social challenges of the 1980s. First-is the following:
Inflation strikes hardest at the old and those least able to take care of themselves.
We announced our intention to introduce legislation that would raise the guaranteed income supplement by $35 a
Old Age Security
month per household beginning July 1 of this year. As the hon. member knows, we have acted promptly in this regard. On May 24, all parties gave approval on third reading to Bill C-16, which proposes amendments to the Old Age Security Act.
The measures endorsed by this House will, as has just been mentioned, provide a $35 a month increase to each pensioner couple currently in receipt of the GIS and spouse's allowance benefits. It should be noted that this increase will be added to the quarterly cost of living increases already provided.
The fact that 1.3 million persons, representing over half the OAS population, receive these income tested benefits indicates that clearly there is prevalence of poverty among elderly Canadians. In effect, this means that all GIS recipients who are unmarried or who are married to persons who are not OAS or spouse's allowance beneficiaries will receive the $35 increase. In the case of a GIS recipient married to another GIS recipient or to a spouse's allowances recipient, each spouse will receive a $17.50 monthly increase so that the over-all increase in benefits will be $35 per household.
I have just described how the government's proposals will benefit current GIS and SPA recipients. I would like to draw the attention of the hon. member to another important aspect of the bill, namely, that an additional 45,000 persons will automatically become entitled to receive these benefits as a result of the increase in the GIS income threshold.
Broadly speaking, the proposals which I have just outlined reflect the government's concern for the economic hardships faced by pensioners on low incomes. For now, hon. members opposite should recognize that Bill C-16 represents an early attempt on our part to provide relief to elderly people who are facing immediate economic hardship.
What about long-term solutions for the retired population as a whole? I want to assure those present today that we are looking beyond immediate solutions in this short term. Indeed, during the course of the debate on Bill C-16, we stated many times that it is our intention to seek solutions to the many pension issues facing us now and in the years ahead.
During the debate we emphasized a commitment to convene a national conference on pensions this fall. This conference is being planned because we know there is a tremendous challenge awaiting us in terms of coming to grips with existing problems in Canada's retirement income system. Make no mistake; I am referring here to problems in both the public sector and in the private sector.
We know, for example, that the system we have is not giving pensioners enough retirement income to maintain their standard of living. It is not giving pensioners enough protection against inflation. It is not meeting the needs of women working in the home or women in the labour force. It is not doing enough for the disabled or the handicapped. It is not protecting the pension rights of workers who change jobs. In short, the system is not doing its job.

June 2, 1980
Old Age Security
This fact is well recognized by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre whose motion today is testimony of his commitment to positive reform. As the hon. member knows, we now have at our disposal a substantial body of well-researched material which identifies problems in the pension system and recommends alternatives. I could point, for example, to the report of the Task Force on Retirement Income Policy, which the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) tabled on April 21.
Among others, the report of the Ontario royal commission which is due this fall will undoubtedly provide important input to the discussions ahead.
So the background research is near completion. What we need now is a forum in which to focus our attention on the options open to us. That is the reason the National Pension Conference will be convened. It will provide such a forum. It will enable us to bring together members of society who represent pensioners, workers, employers, advisory bodies, the pension industry and the various levels of government. We want to obtain their views and to develop a co-ordinated course of action for the reform of the pension system. I should stress that any process of reform will require close consultation with the provincial governments, whose support and co-operation will be vital if the necessary improvements are to be achieved. We hope the result will be the find of adequate and effective pension system that Canadians want and deserve.
I realize I have devoted quite a bit of time in this debate to describing the steps now planned for improving Canada's retirement income system. It seems to me the motion before us cannot, and should not, be considered in isolation from current pension reform initiatives.
In effect, today's motion is, for all practical purposes, identical to the one put forward by the hon. member in January, 1979. This certainly speaks well for the hon. member's tenacity. When that earlier motion was debated on the floor of the House, the hon. member recommended that the basic old age security pension be increased to $350 a month. This time round, I note that the figure has been revised upwards to $400 a month.
I am sure that, in an ideal world of unlimited resources, we would all readily adopt the hon. member's suggestions. However, we all know only too well that these are far from ideal times, in economic terms at least. Our economic resources are limited.
1 was interested to hear the hon. member for Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker) give support to the goals of the motion. However, when the government of which he was a member was in office, I do not believe there were any initiatives along the line we recently demonstrated when we raised the supplement by $35 a month. His party is continually berating this side for the existing deficit, to say nothing of what the deficit would be if this motion were to pass. Our economic resources are limited.
One of the principal messages delivered in the throne speech was that "Canadians recognize the need to live within their
national means, and they understand that in doing so the state cannot meet every demand or satisfy every group." This government would be irresponsible to ignore the economic reality. And so, we are seeking to direct the limited resources available to those who need them most. That is exactly why we have introduced Bill C-16.
In contrast, this motion implies that we should eliminate the guaranteed income supplement program altogether, and opt instead for an increased OAS pension in the amount of $400.
That brings about some serious inequities. For example, assuming the OAS pension were raised to $400, persons now receiving the basic pension of $186.80 would derive a net increase of about $213. Certainly they would be at the low end of the need scale. But what about OAS pensioners who are now entitled to receive the maximum guaranteed income supplement? Already, these persons receive $314 at the married rate and $340 at the single rate. So their net increases would only amount to $86 and $60 respectively.
Over all, those in greatest need would benefit least from this proposal. Instead of narrowing the gap between rich and poor, this measure would cause it to widen considerably.
Aside from the question of equity, the suggestion to raise the basic OAS pension to $400 a month is simply too costly. As mentioned previously, the current OAS benefit is $186.80 a month, which adds up to a cool $5.3 billion a year. That does not including the guaranteed income supplement or the spouse's allowance which, together with the $35 GIS proposed for July, add another $2.2 billion to the over-all projected program budget for 1980-81. Were we to raise the pension to $400 a month, as the hon. member suggests, the annual program costs would skyrocket to $10.8 billion; $3 billion in excess of our projected budget. That figure only reflects the increase which would result if the age criterion remained at 65. If it were reduced to 60, the figure would be astronomical; it would go through the roof. Just imagine the increased costs if we were to follow another of the hon. member's suggestions, namely to pay the pension as early as age 60 to those who are not in the labour force.
In addition, since the Canada Pension Plan is a contributory program, the increased costs of paying earlier benefits would have to be borne by Canadian workers and their employers. We have known since the plan's first inception that the contributory rates would have to rise from the current 3.6 per cent of contributory earnings. Indeed, questions concerning how much this increase will be, and when it will come into effect, are currently being studied by a committee of federal and provincial finance officials. Although their study has not yet been completed, we do know that the contribution rate will have to rise to about 8 per cent over the course of the next half century. And that is the rate projected without major changes to the plan. If, on top of this, you were to add the increased costs resulting from retirement benefits payable at 60, contribution rates would start escalating dramatically. Before passing on that burden to future generations of contributors, I think we would need to weigh carefully the long-term implications of the hon. member's suggestion.
June 2, 1980

I would like to move on, now, to the suggestion that any means test or income test be eliminated from the Old Age Security Act. First, let me clear up any misconceptions here. Neither the guaranteed income supplement nor the spouse's allowance benefit is means-tested, if we define a means test as an examination of both income and assets. Rather, these benefits are determined by an income test, based on the income of the individual as defined by the Income Tax Act. The latter is a more generous approach which enables a pensioner to own assets such as a home, and still remain eligible to receive some financial assistance. It is also a more humane approach in that the individual's personal possessions are at no time subjected to scrutiny, as they would be under means-testing.
But I know the hon. member is more concerned with a discussion of principles, here, than with semantics. What he is really proposing is to raise the old age security benefit and to do away with the income-tested guaranted income supplement and spouse's allowance benefits. In other words, he is questioning the principle that financial assistance should be provided to those in greatest need, a principle which, as I said earlier on in this debate, will be the cornerstone of this government's approach to social policy for some time to come.
Given the limited economic resources available, I think it is fortunate that we have a vehicle such as the guaranteed income supplement program through which the government can continue to direct assistance to those who need it most. As mentioned previously, Bill C-16 will enable us to accomplish this goal.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 note that the hon. member remains committed to automatic indexation of benefits based on some measure of the Canadian standard of living. This point was discussed at some length during the debate on Bill C-16. As we all know, old age security, guaranteed income supplement and spouse's allowance benefits are indexed four times a year, taking into account quarterly increases in the consumer price index. I must say I find the frequency of the increases and the close relationship they bear to recent rises in the cost of living to be two very commendable aspects of these programs. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would probably not agree with me on this issue, but I think it would be very difficult for him to come up with an indexation tool which would be as available as quickly as the consumer price index is. The speed at which the index becomes available is one of the factors which ensures the responsiveness of these programs to the increasing costs of accommodation, food, clothing and so on which our pensioners must face.
One of the most common criticisms of the method we use to index these pension benefits is that the consumer price index is not representative of the increases in the cost of living of pensioners. Critics often say that the basket of goods used to determine increases in that index contains many items which pensioners do not include in their own shopping baskets. Many of them suggest that a separate index should be devised to reflect increases in the costs of items which pensioners actually
Old Age Security
purchase. In response to this suggestion, a number of studies were undertaken by Statistics Canada, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Economic Council of Canada. The Economic Council stated in its 1976 Annual Review that consumer price indices calculated for different income groups deviated only slightly from the price index published by Statistics Canada. The health and welfare study substantiated this finding. Statistics Canada produced an experimental price index for a group of low-income families based on the 1969 family expenditures survey. They found that for the period from June, 1973, to June, 1977, the official CPI had increased to a higher level than the experimental CPI for low-income families. In other words, if the experimental CPI had been used to index pension benefits pensioners would not have been as well off as they actually were when their benefits were increased by the official consumer price index. Incidentally, I understand that Statistics Canada is in the process of analysing data received from the 1978 family expenditures survey. This may reveal a substantial change in the spending patterns of low-income persons and pensioners. If this is so, then perhaps the studies I mentioned might be redone to determine whether the results obtained the first time are still valid.
Other critics of our indexing methods have suggested that benefits be increased in line with changes in other indicators such as average wages and salaries, the average of salaries of persons in five designated categories of workers in the public service, the total disposable income of persons in Canada as measured by taxation data, and so on. On this subject I would like to say to hon. members who are concerned about a quick response to changes in the cost of living that most of these indicators are not available as quickly as the consumer price index, and for a variety of reasons. Wage and salary data is required from employers; contract settlements often take place months after the contract has expired and income tax returns are required only after four months from the end of the taxation years. The use of indicators such as these would involve an even greater time lag than the current method using the C.P.I. Further, I cannot see how salary or tax information could be used to provide quarterly indexation.
In the second place, the goal of the indexation of benefits is to maintain the purchasing power of pension benefits and protect pensioners from the effects of inflation. On the grounds of equity, it would be nice if pensioners could share in the increasing prosperity of the Canadian economy. However, it has been estimated that to increase OAS/GIS benefits according to increases in average wages and salaries would have cost us over $100 million in 1979. As most hon. members know by now, the government has chosen to adopt a policy of granting assistance to persons most in need. Thus, instead of granting assistance to all OAS pensioners-some of whom have enough income to disqualify from receiving GIS-we have chosen to direct funds only to GIS pensioners. If we were to have changed, at this time, the vehicle for indexing benefits, there might not have been sufficient funds for the $35 per household increase that we approved in this chamber last week.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief, but I do want to say a few words about this. I have always worried about giving the government a blank cheque, and that in essence is what we are doing at this time. I can recall on other occasions in another place discussing similar kinds of legislation, and it worries me when the government asks, as it does here and it does traditionally, for authority to go into the marketplace to borrow money at any time subject only to the approval by itself.
The government is saying that it wants us in the House of Commons to allow it go to any part of the world to borrow in whatever amounts it requires up to many billions of dollars- $12 billion, to be exact-and to borrow in funds of any country from which it wishes, and to repay in those same funds. It makes no reference to how it will be responsible to this House. We have to understand that in this year 1980 and into the year 1981 we are dealing in the House of Commons with expenditures of a new government for which there has not yet been a budget.
We are dealing with expenditures of a government which has not yet presented to the House of Commons any indication of how it intends to spend taxpayers' money and how it intends to finance the ongoing programs of government. What we are being asked for today is somewhat unusual. We are being asked, prior to seeing what the government's expenditures are going to be or how it intends to finance its expenditures or how it intends to raise its money or how it intends to pay whatever portion of the deficit it may accumulate over the next 12 months, to authorize extensive borrowing. If not from here, at least from elsewhere my understanding has always been that prior to the government's asking for such authority it normally places before the House of Commons or the representatives of the public its intentions with regard to how it proposes to deal with the finances of the country or of the jurisdiction. We have no budget, we have no economic strategy, we have no clear program for reducing the deficit, and we have no employment strategy. We do not have any idea which area of the world the government intends to turn to in order to do its borrowing. We do not know at what rates of interest it may be interested in borrowing money. We do not know how it intends to pay it back.

speechtext: Thank you. Before the government asks for authority to borrow, they should tell us what it is their budget is likely to contain. That is the first point. speechtext: Blank cheque.

speechtext:
It is funny; that is the term that I used when I started. Had you been here, you would have heard it.
That is what worries me about it. 1 do not see how any government can ask for approval to borrow money until it tells us, at least in general terms, what that money would be used for. I do not see how the government can legitimately expect that the House of Commons would give approval to the government to go out and borrow this money without any understanding of how this government proposes it would repay that, over whatever period of time and in whatever way. I can recall the debate in which I was involved some years ago when the Ontario government borrowed in Germany in Deutschmarks. Perhaps for the first time in the Ontario government's history, it borrowed in foreign currency.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY

Incidentally, those were fiscally irresponsible Conservatives.
I want to suggest that, therefore, when this government puts into this piece of legislation that it should be given the authority to borrow in foreign money markets, you must understand that what the government is saying is that the effective interest rate must also take into account the value of the Canadian dollar in the money market and that the effective interest rate will undoubtedly be considerably higher, if all the current trends continue, than we would expect to pay were we able, with careful management over a period of time, to self-finance.
I want to say to the government that I think this is an inappropriate piece of legislation at this time. At least, I think that portion of this legislation is inappropriate. 1 am not so dumb I cannot understand that governments from time to time require to borrow just as other people do, and I am not pretending for a moment that I do not approve of the government borrowing money from time to time in order to finance long-term projects. 1 am not suggesting for a moment that we

June 2, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
are able in any society to self-finance on an immediate cash flow basis. But I am suggesting that when we see a piece of legislation without knowing exactly the intent of the government with regard to expenditure and revenue, and when we see a piece of legislation which allows for interest rates about which we have no idea, when we get this from a government that has no real control over the monetary policy of the country, and when we see a rapid deterioration of the Canadian dollar against other currencies, and then we see the Canadian economy suffering as it is now suffering at the hands of multinational corporations which frankly do not care that much about what happens in Canada, and when we see people unemployed and unable to pay their share which they must ultimately pay if we are going to be able to repay these loans, and when you see the government bringing in, as it did this afternoon, a piece of legislation dealing with employment which in fact does not even begin to address the major problems which confront the majority of constituencies across the country from the east to the west coast; when you see all of those things happening and you understand that the unemployment that we are currently facing will continue to rise, then you have to ask yourself, where are we going to get this money from and at what rate of interest? What is it that we are going to mortgage away over the next ten or 20 years? I would like to know the answer to some of those questions because, frankly, I believe that it would be better if the government were to come to the House of Commons quarterly and ask for permission to go into the money market and raise whatever capital they require on that basis. 1 would much prefer that we agree to divide this bill so that at the end of the first quarter the government may have borrowed a quarter of what it requires, and at the end of the half year it may borrow another quarter, and so on, so that it is answerable to the House of Commons, having to come back to the House and justify its expenditures and its borrowing, its interest, and the depreciation of the dollar. I am not prepared to say 1 accept as a matter of course that the government will handle this borrowing appropriately, that it will not misuse it as it has in the past, that it will borrow with care and consideration, that it will get the very best deals, and that analysts will do an analysis of what the money trends will be at this time as opposed to what they were last time. Quite frankly. 1 feel that this piece of legislation, although no doubt it is necessary to give the government power to borrow, is asking for too long a period. 1 do not deny that it may be
tradition in the House of Commons, but tradition is something we can change. It asks for too much too soon. I would much rather the government reconsider it and came back with a piece of legislation which enabled us in the House of Commons to look much more critically and much more carefully, not only at the expenditures, but at the way in which it is going into the marketplace, the rates of interest, and the actual total dollars it would have to pay. For those reasons I feel very reluctant to see this piece of legislation passed.

No; as a matter of fact 1 won. In fact the message from western Canada was very clear. One of the obligations 1 must fulfil is to express the concern that at least western Canadians feel about the size of government. In the last campaign I campaigned largely on the basis of fiscal responsibility based on restraint in government spending and a gradual reduction of the national deficit. That was the basis of every speech I made. It was the basis of my campaign material, and the basis upon which the people of my constituency voted for me. Therefore, it is absolutely essential that I should stand up and object when in fact the people of my riding in western Canada are getting just the opposite.
Extending the authority of government to borrow lessens the will, the necessity and the capacity of government to repay and work toward balanced budgets and reduced national debt. In 1980 western Canadians voted against increased government spending and deficits. They voted for an end to the paternalistic control and domination of the manufacturing base of central Canada and domination of the manufacturing base of central Canada and the federal government. Somehow in western Canada there was in fact a double protest vote this time. It was more than just against large central government; it was against the paternalistic central control of big government. I think that needs to be recognized particularly at this time in the House.
This is a bill which further centralizes economic power through the onerous burden of escalating national debt. This bill can only add more fuel to an already growing sense of western alienation. The roots of western alienation or separation are complex and difficult to express. The roots are historical, geographical, sociological, emotional, traditional, but, above all, the roots of separatism in the west are economic. Western alienation is not a new phenomenon. Perhaps in the past the roots have been a bit dry and weak, but in the 1980s, watered by new economic powers in the west, they are blossoming forth with an identity that must be listened to, and must be understood. This must be responded to in the same way that Quebec has been heard and, hopefully, will be responded to, again with more than this traditional paternal pat on the head with some token words about responsible
June 2, 1980

Canadianism. Somehow in the west we are not supposed to say anything. It is somehow unCanadian if this comes from the west.
Specifically, what are the kinds of things the west is talking about? The question always comes up: "What are you complaining about? Do not tell us you are mad, angry, upset or that you do not like this. What specifically do you want?" Of course the question of oil pricing is paramount. But just to list a few, there is interference in the resource control management, unfair freight rate systems, inadequate transportation systems, inadequate incentives to process upstream, that syndrome of the hewers of wood and drawers of water. In addition there is insufficient access to the United States and Pacific rim markets in terms of the products we produce, lack of secondary industry and lack of representation on national boards and institutions. Somehow in the west they feel the great potential that is there is wasted, unrealized and held back. The reality is that westerners feel at this time politically impotent, ignored and exploited by both Ottawa and Bay Street.
Central Canadians have dominated the Canadian economic and political scene for so long it seems to anyone who comes from the west to central Canada that everybody believes it is his natural right to continue to do so. But I want to tell this House that central Canadian feudalism ended with the total rejection of the Liberals in western Canada, just as surely as it ended in Quebec with the election of Rene Levesque.

At that time I was pleased with the response. The potential of the west is just beginning to show as is the potential of the Pacific rim. I could list so many things in Vancouver and British Columbia that do not need subsidies. We are not looking for a subsidy mentality in British Columbia; we are looking for an investment mentality. We are looking for a recognition of investment in the Pacific rim. We are looking for a new face, a new western face for Canada. That is why the initiative started with the Pacific conference was good. One of the architects of the bill is from the west. We want a trade and convention centre that can be a showcase on the Pacific face of Canada.
Somehow, in western Canada we get the feeling that we are a bunch of lumberjacks or something, and there is nothing wrong with that. We are very proud to be the lumberjacks of
Canada, the hewers of wood and drawers of water. Those are things to be proud of. Premier Bennett says, "Energy resources will be the cornerstone of his province's growth strategy for the 1980s, but if the federal government dips into the B.C. gas revenues, it could mean a further $50 million penalty to the people of B.C. and it could make it difficult for us to carry out our policy of lessening our dependence on oil.
Borrowing Authority Act
These aspirations are not hard to understand, nor are they anything but reasonable and responsible under any form of renewed federalism. Provincial control of resources is seen as the primary instrument to redress the balance. But recent federal actions and court decisions challenge their control. Only western resources are singled out to be sold in Canada at less than world prices. No one imposes a federal export tax on Ontario or Quebec exports of hydro energy. No one subsidized Saskatchewan when it had to pay four or five times the Ontario price for electricity. No one in the east suggested a national subsidy or equalization of gas prices when it was more expensive in the west than in the east. That is very real among the people on the street.
There are those in the government who have the fantasy of twinning with members from the west. I wish you would come out west and hear what is being said. This bill thwarts the aspirations of the west by overcommitting the tax resource of Canada to the federal government. Any hope that moneys accruing to the federal government would be returned to develop the resource potential of the west seems slim indeed- in fact, even slimmer as I stand here tonight and listen to the response of the government. Almost all the evidence so far indicates that the fat eastern standard and the slim western standard continue with such things as subsidies, protective tariffs, government waste, central government patronage and so forth.
Let me give an example. This House was in an absolute crisis for two weeks while we worried about the jobs in the car industry. It is good that this House should worry and should be concerned. The government came forth with a guarantee of $200 million. That $200 million would provide a ratio of $1 billion in investment and would save 15,000 jobs. At the time there were discussions that Ontario's contribution would be between $10 million and $50 million. 1 want hon. members to remember those figures because they represent the eastern standard.
Now, let us look at the western standard. We are not talking about $1 billion in investment, but about $5 billion, five times as much, for developing the coal industry in British Columbia. They are talking about $75 million on a $1 billion investment. The federal government offers some $70 million and expects the British Columbia government to pick up the rest. The British Columbia government is forced to say "I guess we will have to go it alone as usual". That is the kind of standard this government has toward the west. Based on the eastern standard of five to one, the government should invest $1 billion to British Columbia's $5 billion.
if the government were to do that it would not just be subsidizing or maintaining jobs that are questionable, but investing in the most viable industry in the world right now, the energy resource industry, and the great coal resource of British Columbia. But you drag your feet, and when you come out west you cannot understand why the British Columbia government complains. Too often it seems that not much has changed since 1938 when the then government of British Columbia stated that approximately 80 per cent of the manufactured commodities imported into B.C. are from eastern Canada while 75 per cent of our main primary products are sold in open competition in the world markets. The largest market in the world, the Pacific Rim, is sitting there waiting for Canada to begin to participate.
The majority of people who I represent do not want to join the Collver movement to join the United States. They do not want to separate from Canada. What they want is to rejoin Canada, and 78 per cent want a new deal, a better deal for British Columbia and all the regions within confederation. Central to these very real aspirations is the sanctity of the resource base as a building block toward growth in the west. How can Canada assume this vast new debt we are talking about tonight, unless there is some thought in the cabinet of trying to steal the resource base revenue of western Canada?
If this government feels that somehow it received a mandate in the last election to equalize, steal, take, borrow or share the resource base of western Canada in another form of equalization, they completely missed the message and they have completely underestimated the depth of the feelings held by most western Canadians. This is the kind of miscalculation that could lead to severe stress and a break up of this nation. Surely the government learned from the Quebec referendum and from the 1980 election that the message of both Quebec and British Columbia is that it must respect the aspirations of the regions of Canada.
If the government forces this bill through the House and proceeds to borrow more and spend more because it has a majority government, then it will only lead to trouble. You throw good money after bad in subsidizing uneconomic industries in central Canada, and fail to develop the secondary
industrial base of western Canada. Surely some of that money, and we are talking about billions of dollars, should be spent on new jobs and new industries in western Canada.
When the minister responds, if he does, let him tell us how he plans to do this. We hear this request echoed here and over there. What we are concerned about is, being asked to pass the bill before we have heard what the bill is going to do. Would the minister stand up and tell me that the government is going to recognize the potential of the west and is going to develop the secondary industry, that it is going to work in partnership with British Columbia to develop a common front that it will meet the entrepreneurs of the Pacific rim, the Japanese, the Asian nation representatives and develop the west?
Talk about the excitement of the west; it is an exciting frontier and it has an exciting potential. If the minister can tell me that he is going to do those things and tell me how much money the government is going to give us to do it, then I might have to reconsider my position. History has told us that that will not happen. 1 hope history can be proven wrong.
My hon. colleagues who spoke before me have already asked this question again and again. I wonder if it will be heard. The government does not choose to tell us what it is going to do with the $12 billion. This is the same group that defeated the Conservative budget then promptly reintroduced most of its measures. This is the same group that protested interest rates while in opposition and let them rise unimpeded once they returned to their cosy chairs on the other side. This is the same crew who criticized the Conservative finance minister for seeking borrowing authority before introducing a budget. The same bunch is asking us in Parliament and the Canadian people to trust them. "Trust us", they say, "and we will look after you". They have certainly looked after us. They have done such a good job that they are asking us for more money than ever before to bail them out of the huge deficit of their own making.
The interest on the public debt has grown at an average rate of 17.7 per cent over the period 1969 to 1979. It has increased at a rate of 22 per cent since 1974. So the Liberal government has looked after us since 1979, to the point that interest costs amount to 15.4 per cent of federal government expenditure. The record is tragic indeed.
The Conservative government was going to operate on a borrowing requirement of $8.2 billion for a full fiscal year, yet still offering within that package a mortgage and property tax credit. The people of my riding voted for those too.

I am introducing a private member's bill. As part of the legislative program. It seeks to limit federal government expenditure to a fixed percentage of the gross national product. With this I would hope to ensure that government spending would always be present to ensure a proper functioning of the economy without being so great as to stifle productivity.
Until we realize that government spending will not cure all of our ills, that massive borrowing will not solve problems it created in the first place; until that time comes one cannot expect to realize the full economic potential which our country possesses. In response to the comments being made at the moment by hon. members opposite, 1 suggest that is the reason the hon. member for St. John's West waited some seven months before bringing down his budget.
There are complicated issues of expenditure planning which must be resolved. There is the envelope system of expenditure management which was established by the previous government. I believe this system is a major improvement over its predecessor, however if it is to function properly, the cabinet committees involved must be given time to prepare strategic plans and carefully consider the issues before a fiscal plan is finalized by cabinet. Hon. members opposite are surely aware of the time it takes to resolve a matter of this importance.
Another difficult issue is that of energy pricing. I need not remind hon. members that the previous government sought to establish an energy price agreement with the provinces and still had not succeeded in finalizing it some seven months after taking office. The present government is now involved in the process of negotiation with the energy producing provinces. It is important not to create an atmosphere which will make the negotiations more difficult.

The minister will table his budget when he feels these matters have been dealt with satisfactorily. The financial strategy of the government will be part of this budget. I cannot predict just when the minister will table his budget. For the time being, however, I should like to return to the reasons we are seeking authority to borrow $12 billion. In his statement of April 21, the Minister of Finance indicated that he expected financial requirements of $11.7 billion for the fiscal year 1980-81. This figure was based on the current structure of revenue and expenses. The minister had also emphasized that setting up a blended price system for oil could in itself reduce the financial requirements by up to $1 billion. Should this saving occur, it is clear that the financial requirements could come down to $10.7 billion. Therefore, the financial requirements range from $10.7 and $11.7 billion.

We are seeking a $12 billion borrowing authority to allow us to meet these financial requirements and to allow us some margin for contingencies. 1 believe it would not make much sense for the government to plan to seek borrowing authority more frequently than once a year. Hon. members will have adequate opportunities to debate on the estimates and on the budget, to express their views on the government's financial policies without having to allocate scarce parliamentary time to a more frequent consideration of borrowing authority bills.
I turn now to answers to some specific questions raised by the hon. member for St. John's West. Then I will turn to answer some specific questions raised by other hon. members.

1 am sure the hon. member can appreciate that in financing the cash requirement the amount of cash raised through the issue of various types of security in Canada varies from year to year and depends on prevailing economic and financial conditions. The actual debt program for the past two fiscal years illustrates how the cash requirements have been met in the past. This is illustrated in a table entitled Cash Requirement and Sources of Financing which I intend to have tabled in the House.
In 1978-79 foreign exchange transactions substantially reduced the cash requirements and the $8.8 billion debt program resulted in a $1.9 billion addition to cash balance. In fiscal 1979-80 foreign exchange transactions had almost no impact on cash requirements and these were financed by a run-down in cash balances which had been built up in the previous year and a $7.9 billion debt program. In 1979-80 a greater use was made of treasury bills and marketable bonds than in 1978-79 and there were net redemptions of CSBs over the fiscal year. In fiscal 1980-81 we do not plan to make much use of cash balances to finance cash requirements. Consequently, we plan to raise all the cash requirements in the capital market. Since the government has for some time being playing down the role of Canada Savings Bonds we do not expect to raise much new money from this source during fiscal 1980-81. We have also been making more use of the treasury bill market in this year. Consequently, we expect that the proportion of the debt program met through the issue of treasury bills will be larger than in the past two fiscal years and the proportion met through issue of marketable bonds will be closer to that in fiscal 1978-79.
[ Translation]
The hon. member asked what we intended to do about the Canada Saving Bonds and about the volume of redemptions that the government could absorb. I agree with the hon.

June 2, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
member that the government should continue to resort less to CSB issues and that is exactly what it has been doing since 1974. The proportion of outstanding CSB issues relative to the whole amount of the debt in Canadian dollars has dropped from a high of 43 per cent in 1975 to somewhere in the range of 27 per cent now.

The hon. member asked how many CSB redemptions we can absorb. So far this fiscal year net redemptions have amounted to about $1.3 billion and this amount has been paid out of our cash balances. In recent weeks we have offset virtually all of this cash drain through our borrowing operations in marketable securities. Very recently net CSB redemptions have fallen off rather sharply, which to a large extent reflects the sharp decline in interest rates that has largely eliminated the gap between interest rates payable on competing financial instruments and on outstanding CSB issues. We expect that the CSB redemption problem is over.
The hon. member for St. John's West also asked how much of the government's indebtedness was in the form of various types of instruments, how much was short-term debt, how much long-term debt and how much is payable in foreign currencies. The answers to these questions are provided in the Bank of Canada Review. However, I will briefly provide an outline of the current debt structure as at the end of March, 1980.

While 1 cannot forecast who will buy the government's securities over the balance of this fiscal year, the following table, which I will read to the House, provides the distribution and changes in holdings of marketing securities for 1979-80 and up to March 21 of this year. As of March 31, 1980, the Bank of Canada held 14.6 per cent of the domestic marketable
Government of Canada securities. As of May 21 of this year it held 12.7 per cent, a drop of 1.9 percentage points. The government accounts held 1 per cent as of March 31, 1980, and as of May 21, 1980, it was down to .9 per cent. Chartered banks held 9.7 per cent as of March 31, and as of May 21 held 10 per cent, an increase of .3 per cent. The general public held 24.5 per cent on March 31, 1980, and now it holds 27.9 per cent as of May 21.
As the figures reflect, the major purchases of government debt this fiscal year and the last have been by the general public. So far in 1980-81 the Bank of Canada has been a substantial net seller of Government of Canada securities.
The hon. member for St. John's West has stated that the interest costs on the foreign debt last October were $326 million and has asked what they are now and what are the net interest costs.
In answer to the first question, these interests costs are substantially unchanged from what they were last October. The specific net interest costs, however, are difficult to determine at this time. To the extent that the foreign currencies raised by these loans are maintained in official exchange reserves they are invested in short-term U.S. dollar government securities. To the extent that the U.S. dollars are converted to Canadian dollars through foreign exchange operations the Canadian dollars are deposited with Canadian chartered banks where they earn 90 per cent of the current Treasury bill rate. In this latter case, government cash balances are increased, and this offsets the need to borrow in Canada.
Most of the foreign currency loans were made in 1978 and early 1979, and since official U.S. dollar reserves are currently around $1.8 billion, most of the proceeds are either deposited with Canadian banks where they currently earn around 10.35 per cent or have been spent to offset borrowing in Canada at current high levels.
The U.S. dollars in official reserves earn interest at a level of around 8 per cent. Much of the interest cost on foreign loans is below these levels.
With that as a background and in an attempt to respond as fully as possible to the questions raised by the hon. member for St. John's West I would like to turn to commenting on some of the questions raised by other hon. members, first of all the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) in his statements on Bill C-30 late last week. Rather interestingly, in this new Parliament what has now been given to us in the economic statement is an indication that the federal level of spending in relation to the gross national product will grow by 2 per cent in one year from approximately 20 per cent of the gross national product to 22 per cent of the gross national product.
This is simply not true. As the hon. member for Edmonton East will see when the budget is presented, federal government

expenditures or a percentage of GNP will remain in the same range they have been in since 1975.

I was very interested in the content of the speech of the parliamentary secretary. He is quite right when he talks about the difference between the net debt and the gross debt. As hon. members know, in fiscal 1980 the net debt amounts to $67 billion as I understand it. This is the gross public debt minus certain assets. These assets normally include such items as repayable loans to Crown corporations and national governments and equity investments like Petro-Canada and the Canadian Development Corporation. But I believe that in fiscal 1980 the gross debt was $105 billion which indeed is a great deal of money. Following what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) said, I also understand that the gross public debt charges for fiscal 1981 will amount to $10.3 billion and as I think he said tonight, 17.7 per cent of budgetary expenditures.
These matters are very esoteric to most of us. I do not pretend to understand all the subtleties of finance. 1 was always told that if your outgo exceeds your income, your upkeep will be your downfall. I understand that, but also I understand that there has been a great increase in the total amount of public debt since I first came to this place nine years ago. Whether we get into proportions of debt or not, vis-a-vis the GNP, it is fair to say by way of emphasis that the amount of the deficit now is as much as the total budget was when 1 first came here. Whether or not this is as alarming as it sometimes seems when one relates it to the proportion of the GNP, I leave that to the judgment of my peers here in the House. But nonetheless it is a striking figure.
In looking for historical parallels and wondering just how the Liberal party conducted financial affairs in its early days, I looked at Canadian Quotations and Phrases, Literary and Historical. That is not hysterical, but historical, compiled by Robert M. Hamilton. Wanting to be fair and equitable, 1 looked through the section on the Liberal party, wanting to

I was fortunate enough to come across something which was featured in a supplementary to The Montreal Gazette, a paper with which Mr. Speaker is familiar, back in 1891. The hon. parliamentary secretary, to do him some justice, answered a lot of questions, but he quite properly added in response to comments from this side of the House that of course there are some details which have to be filled in yet. However I think one of the things he said that is interesting before we get to that stage, was the bit of information which he gave us, if I took it down properly, that we owe $4.7 billion or close to $5 billion to foreign countries payable in their own currencies. Having in mind the state of the Canadian dollar relative to most of the countries where we do our borrowing these days, such as the United States, Switzerland and West Germany, I presume that that $4.7 billion in effect means a lot more indebtedness than it would first appear. To be fair about it, I suppose there must be a discount there of at least 15 or maybe 20 per cent when we have to pay those funds back.
When the parliamentary secretary is answering more questions, as he indicated he would do, I wonder if he might give us the premium we will have to pay. This leads me back to the point the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) made in his speech as to why we need that particular, explicit authority in clause 2 of the bill, if we have already managed to incur that kind of a debt. Perhaps it is related to trade, 1 do not know. As you know, Your Honour, subsection 2 states very clearly that this government does want authority, for greater certainty that they can borrow, in effect, currency other than that of Canada. I would hope that until our currency improves a little bit more in terms of its relative value to most others they would not avail themselves of that option-that if they already have it they would refrain from doing it and that if they get it, they will use it very carefully.
I think it was the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in his always quiet, persuasive way, who pointed out that we were away behind value in most currencies in the world, including the Zambian kwacha. Whether we owe any Zambian kwachas or not, I do not know but 1 hope not.
i believe that in considering the large amount of money this government is requesting-and properly so-it would be in order for a member such as myself to make some suggestions about how some of this money-which is about $5 billion more than the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West required last fall-might better be spent by this administration as they bring forth their budget and prepare their special estimates.
It seems to me, for example, that recent events on the international scene indicate very clearly that if there is one place where the Canadian people would find it advisable to see their hard-earned, borrowed money, spent, it would be in the improvement of the capabilities of this country to defend itself and to take a proper place in the defence of the western world.
1 know these figures have been put on the record before and 1 do not propose to take up much of the time of the House but it seems that when talking about GNP, percentage of spending and so on, these figures issued by the Institute of Strategic Studies in London on the military balance which are fairly new, might be interesting to hon. members.
The percentage of government spending of our budget in 1979 was 8.6 per cent, less than it has taken to service our national indebtedness by far. On the other hand, the United States which carries the burden of our western defence, spent 21.6 per cent; the United Kingdom 11.5 per cent; the Netherlands 9.1 per cent; Sweden, a supposedly neutral country, 8.4 per cent and Czechoslovakia 7.1 per cent. 1 know it is very difficult to precisely relate the percentages for some countries, particularly those in the eastern bloc which sometimes bury their military expenditures in other ways.
The percentage of the GNP, which is another way of expressing the priorities of these countries that I picked out at random in reporting their military spending, indicates that 1.8 per cent is all that this country spends; United States 5 per
