cent; United Kingdom 4.7 per cent; The Netherlands 3.3 per cent; Sweden 3.4 per cent and Czechoslovakia 3.8 per cent. It is evident we are not doing our part. We are a nation, small in population, that controls a very large percentage of the real estate on this planet and a disproportionate amount of its natural resources. I say to you and to my colleagues, Mr. Speaker, that unless we are kidding ourselves we cannot believe that we can even patrol the treasure house we have in the north, much less defend it.
1 certainly hope in considering what is going to be done with these funds the government is asking Parliament for, that very serious consideration be given to doing something about protecting the future of this part of the continent. If one can take seriously the reports emanating from different parts of the world, the Soviet Union is now in a very, very interesting position. Their military machinery, their electronic capability, the relative disarray of the west, puts them in the position where, between now and 1985, they might be very tempted indeed to go to some other type of military adventure.
Surely every country in the western world including ours, in particular, as we are so close to the United States and so deficient in meeting our own defence commitment, has an obligation to do something quickly to send out signals showing that we are prepared to act.
Henry Kissinger was interviewed for an article in Time magazine recently. As he was one of the principal architects of detente it is interesting to note that he said it is absolutely imperative to get across to the Soviet Union that their definition of detente is simply unacceptable. He said their definition of detente is to be committed to defeat the United States peacefully and that they would either have to accept that they could not undertake a geo-political offensive or would have to give up detente. He went on to list some of what the Soviet Union has done since 1975: Cuban troops in Angola; Cuban troops in Ethiopia; Soviet bases in South Yemen, Ethiopia and Libya; for the past few years the Soviet occupations of Afghanistan, the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia under the cover of a friendship treaty, and a Soviet brigade in Cuba which he claimed happened after 1976 no matter what nonsense is being put out.
In a recent magazine article Maclean's magazine reminded us of the grizzly anniversary of the massacre in Katyn Forest in Poland which up to this point the Soviet Union has tried to blame on Nazi Germany. It is becoming clear that it was perpetrated by the Soviets.
I only mention these things to show that in my humble opinion there is much to be said for the definition that Winston Churchill gave of Soviet diplomacy at a time when he was holding all parliamentarians enthralled with his picturesque and accurate speeches in various parts of the western world. I do not know where it was he made the observation that the Soviet Union's diplomacy is like a burglar in a hotel: They go down the hall trying every door until they find one that is open.
The detente policy and the way we have been conducting ourselves has been an open-door policy but the doors have all
Business of the House
been opened into our resources. 1 believe that some $60 billion has been loaned to the Soviet Union by western financial institutions. I doubt if they can service the interest on that debt, since we are talking large figures tonight, so what is going to happen about that?
1 am trying not to stray too far from the bill before us, Mr. Speaker. I want to make my feelings known to hon. members opposite, however, regarding the priorities they might seek to establish for this rather large amount of money they are asking this House to give them.
Regarding another priority, 1 should like to quote some words of the parliamentary secretary-"a vibrant regional development priority"-or policy, 1 believe is what he said. As he said, we cannot have it both ways-we cannot cut the budget and spend money at the same time. We can re-examine our priorities, however, even if it is almost a cliche to say that it is a good idea to spend money in order to make money.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane), whose aims and philosophies I support, spoke eloquently in this House in a rather unusual fashion not long ago when he made a public plea to his peers for more money for regional development. It is interesting to note that in the priorities of this government, this department, which is perhaps the newest major department to be created in the last ten years, was once the recipient of about 2 per cent of the budgetary allotment of the government; it is now barely half that. Its thrust has been changed. The legislation that governs its use is becoming almost obsolete. Surely the RDIA, which is the basis for these grants, must be changed to bring them in line with different practice and to make sure there is adequate lead time to do this. The minister knows this and I knew it when 1 was minister. We were proceeding to bring forward legislation to improve the operations of DREE. That is not enough, however; additional funds will have to be found for DREE if it is going to continue to have a useful role in developing this country.
It is ironic that the transfer payments have been going up dramatically while DREE declines. That is not all bad, but the amount available for DREE has been going down, which shows again that the proportion of money that this government has available to create the wealth which some departments are so anxious, and properly so, to distribute to our people; that this amount of money is disproportionately larger than the amount of money which goes to departments like Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE to develop our country.
Surely this is a situation that must be looked at in the context of the large amount of money which is being borrowed. As large as the deficit is and as large as the amount which is being borrowed is, I am not as concerned about the fact that it is being borrowed as I am about the way in which it will be spent. Sometimes in the past I think that this government had an edifice complex, not an oedipus complex, and that has to stop. These fine and imposing buildings like the Bank of Canada building, are very nice and very energy inefficient, but they do not do much for the productivity of our country. The

subtopic: CIVIL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR NEW EMPHASIS ON POLICIES AND INCREASED BUDGET
CIVIL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR NEW EMPHASIS ON POLICIES AND INCREASED BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and indeed the Prime Minister of Japan have all stood before this House and warned that we are entering a dangerous decade fraught with instabilities and deteriorating super power relations. The global build-up of arms is a reality. Widespread proliferation of weapons and technology is becoming an increasing reality. The accelerated efforts of both our friends and potential foes to provide protection for their civilians against nuclear threat is a further reality.
We are all charged to work toward global peace, and we can take pride in the fact that Canada's history as a peacemaker is internationally recognized. But to pretend that the nuclear holocaust will not or cannot happen is to lose touch with reality. Worse still, it is shirking our responsibility as members of Parliament toward the people of Canada.
It is certainly not the fault of the Canadian people that civil defencS is so misunderstood. In other countries of the world governments have ensured that their people have the maximum amount of safety and are well versed in emergency measures in the case of nuclear war. I am sure that many hon. members saw the television show on Sweden which talked in part about the underground parking lots which were built to also act as fall-out shelters. Yugoslavia, Finland. Norway and Switzerland have similar programs for their citizens. China has the capacity to move most of its millions of citizens in Peking underground in a matter of minutes.
It is reported that the Soviet Union has spent $65 billion on civil defence in the last ten years. In the United States new plans are being announced and accelerated for mass evacuation of cities in the event of a world crisis. In Britain recently, the House of Lords devoted seven hours of debate to the subject of civil defence. The French Senate called recently for a new and accelerated program for their nation.
However, we in Canada still cannot find out who is the minister of civil defence. In fact, we find that all ministers are ministers for civil defence, but no one is really in charge of civil defence policy and planning. There is no mention of what are the roles of the members of Parliament, the cabinet ministers, the municipal government or the provincial government. It is all very muddy and unclear with each government shifting the buck back and forth.
There is far too much at stake to allow this kind of indifference and this state of unorganization. A congressional committee in the United States estimated that in the event of a nuclear attack on targets in the United States only, there would be two million casualties in Canada. At the present time in our current state of preparedness, a nuclear attack on Canada as well would wipe out over half the population of this country-over half of 23 million people, which amounts to 11 million Canadians. That number could be reduced considerably if the government were to take appropriate action similar to any of the other allies or even our potential enemies.
Some military people say we are being optimistic with those terrible statistics. They argue that Canadian cities would be prime targets. If there were in fact nine prime targets in Canada, that could be a threat to half of our population. If 100 people were threatened and we knew about it in this House of Commons, we would be outraged and calling for action right now.
I direct this question to you, Mr. Speaker. Do you know what you would do if a nuclear bomb were to drop in downtown Montreal? Would you know how to direct the citizens in your riding? Would any member in this House of Commons know what to do as a responsible leader in his community if there were a nuclear attack? I do not think so. I do not think the person who will respond to me can tell me even after he has researched the subject.
We are in an appalling state of affairs with respect to civil defence in Canada. The Prime Minister knows where to go. He has told us; he has his bunker. Some of the cabinet know. They have their protection. There are about 7,000 people out of 23 million who can find a place of reasonable safety in a nuclear war. But what about the other 23 million? There is no place for them, no protection for them and there is no plan for them.
We spend billions of dollars. We just spent $4 billion on planes, guns and tanks. How much do we spend on civil defence, I think it is $1.9 million. The figure is about $2 million. The ratio in $2 million to $4 billion, the amount spent
June 2, 1980

for planes. Civil defence has become a nonentity in Canada unfortunately.
For the past seven years since October, 1973, when the Government of Canada announced that there would be changes in the emergency planning structure within the federal government, there has been almost deadening silence about what the government intends to do. One of the problems stems from the fact that no single minister of the Crown has clear responsibility for civil defence preparedness. Heightening the difficulties is the division of responsibility among the federal government, the provinces and municipalities. Perhaps civil defence must be decentralized. But surely this refers only to the post-attack phase, not to the program policy-making and planning that precedes a nuclear war. To slough off responsibility on to the provinces is to abdicate one of the primary roles of a central government-of any government-to protect its citizens in time of war.
It is clear that the federal government is passing the buck in terms of its responsibilities for civil defence.
The Prime Minister on Friday, May 16, said that he had not received a request for increased civil defence funds nor did he believe that increased funding was necessary. Where has he been among the leaders of the world? I would not like to say that the Prime Minister was misleading. He did not seem to be referring to the true facts of the situation. The Prime Minister did not mention that the federal government has undercut the federal-provincial financial assistance programs to such an extent that the provinces today can scarcely devote any attention to war preparedness. Yet, the Deputy Prime Minister in his response last Wednesday placed the responsibility for implementing existing civil defence plans, such as they were, firmly in the hands of the provinces.
Is the Prime Minister aware of the fact that the Department of National Defence is responsible for establishing public information programs for use in an emergency-just brought up to date-and that the emergency broadcasting system is not reinstated? Their siren system must be enlarged to provide coverage for expanded urban communities, and evacuation plans need to be established in our major cities in any type of war.
There are so many things that need to be done. Canada is not ready. Canada's concern for its citizens must come up to that shown by other countries of the world. Other countries have shown a desire to face the unfortunate reality. It is time that Canada did the same.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: CIVIL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR NEW EMPHASIS ON POLICIES AND INCREASED BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement that responsibility for detailed implementation of the necessary plans is in the hands of the provinces, and that public works and national defence are the federal departments having the most direct responsibility, is indeed correct. Public Works Canada has responsibility for carrying out planning at the federal level for protection of the population of Canada against the war time effects of radioactive fall-out from nuclear weapons. This work is being carried out under the national shelter program. At the present time,
Adjournment Debate
emphasis is being given to completing surveys of fall-out protection inherent in existing buildings.
Information collected by these surveys is made available to provinces and includes the levels of fall-out protection in existing buildings throughout Canada and the people capacities of these buildings, having regard for natural ventilation and physically usable space. These data together with detailed population distribution by city block and small area, constitute the key ingredients to development of both provincial master shelter plans and the more detailed community shelter plans. The work of planning for protection of people certainly points to significant involvement by provinces and communities as well as the federal government.
Provincial master shelter plans and community shelter plans already exist for New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, but the major planning work for the rest of the country has yet to be accomplished, and this can only be achieved if the provinces concerned are willing to co-operate actively in the planning. Although the major survey work across Canada is expected to be completed by the end of 1980, it will take significant effort and resources to bring to fruition the balance of the necessary plans and arrangements that would reduce the vulnerability of Canadians to the effects of radioactive fall-out under nuclear war conditions.
The hon. member opposite decries the confusion and lack of ability of the various jurisdictions to get together. Perhaps the hazard that he speaks of, the threat that he calls to mind as a result of changing world conditions may motivate the various jurisdictions in this country to pull together. At a time when the first ministers are getting together to talk to a total review of our constitution and governmental arrangements, this question is timely and should be on the agenda as this level of government considers its role vis-a-vis the other levels of government.
In conclusion, civil defence cannot be solely a federal responsibility. Provinces and municipalities must of necessity be involved in development of emergency plans affecting the health and well-being of people, whether they be wartime emergencies or peacetime emergencies.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REUNIFICATION OF FAMILIES- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.S.R.
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REUNIFICATION OF FAMILIES- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 20 the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille), speaking from the government side of this House, moved the following motion:
That this House strongly urge the Soviet government to fulfil its undertakings in regard to the provisions of the Helsinki Final Act, specifically those calling for the reunification of families, and to allow the Jewish refusenik. Lev Ovsishcher, to emigrate to Israel.
The motion was seconded by the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), a member of my party. I congratulate the House because the motion received unanimous consent, which is unusual. That indicates some expression of regard for the

June 2, 1980
Adjournment Debate
seriousness of the issue that was raised. On May 26, 1 raised the matter in a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). 1 would like to speak for a moment about Lev Ovsishcher. He was born in Russia in 1919 and was raised as a boy in the city of Minsk. When he was 17 years of age, in 1936, he enlisted in the Soviet army in which he served loyally and with distinction for the next 25 years. He rose to the rank of colonel and retired from the army in 1961.
It is a sad commentary on human events that today in the Soviet Union it would appear to be government policy to denigrate the patriotism of Soviet Jews. Colonel Ovsishcher's military record was outstanding. He was wounded in action at Stalingrad and fought in many of the major battles on the Russian front, including the defence of Moscow. At the end of the war he had received 17 medals for extraordinary bravery and efficiency as a soldier in the terrible struggle to repel the Nazi enemy,
Colonel Ovsishcher emphasized the patriotism of Russian Jews in a speech he made in 1976 quoting statistics well known to the Soviet government. He pointed out that more than half a million Soviet Jews bore arms against the enemy during World War II. Of these, 150 rose to the rank of general. One hundred and seventy thousand Russian Jews were awarded medals or citations for bravery and 160 received the title "Hero of the Soviet Union" for extraordinary valor and devotion to duty. These Jews fought for their homeland, Russia. To us, it seems extraordinary that today only because some of them wish the right to emigrate to Israel they should be cast as traitors to the state.
Colonel Ovsishcher applied for an exit visa to Israel in 1972 and stated his desire to emigrate to that country. The harassment which has become commonplace in such cases commenced immediately. He was deprived of his rank of colonel. He was demoted in his place of employment. His mail was intercepted, his telephone calls disrupted and in 1973 his telephone service was discontinued. Government agents searched his apartment, Yiddish and Hebrew books were confiscated and he was interrogated numerous times by the KGB.
Colonel Ovsishcher defiantly reminded the authorities of his civil rights under the constitution. The harassment continued and in June, 1975, he was advised that he would not be allowed to leave for Israel for at least another three years. As of today, he is still not allowed to emigrate to Israel, unable to join his daughter who is now there.
After the war ended, Colonel Ovsishcher returned to his home in Minsk where in March, 1943, the Nazis executed 5,000 Russian Jews. He and other veterans erected a memorial to that evil act in memory of the victims. This year, as in past years, ceremonies were planned at the site of the memorial; they were especially significant as it was the thirty-fifth anniversary of the defeat of Hitler's Nazi regime. Colonel Ovsishcher was to have attended but was prevented from doing so by the KGB.
On March 6 of this year, with the help of friends in Canada and Russia, 1 was able, along with others, to put a telephone call through to Colonel Ovsishcher from my Vancouver office to him in Minsk. We later received from him a moving letter which reads in part:
I want to express my gratitude to you for your help in our difficult life and for your support which you have shown in your telephone call of March 6. The fact that you have not forgotten us in our hard fight is so important, not only for me but for many other families who are now in the same situation. You know, one man alone can be very weak but we are strong because we know we have supporters and friends. This is what gives us faith that we shall overcome.
When the war against the Nazis was over, we hoped victory would bring us not only peace but also human rights. Unfortunately, it was not so and today the voices of suffering people from many countries ring in the free world asking for your help. It is very important for us that you may hear and listen to these voices.
We must not break faith with Colonel Ovsishcher and the suffering peoples of whom he speaks. I urge the government to convey to the government of the U.S.S.R. the unanimous motion of this House and the remarks which I have had the privilege of making in this House of freedom, the Parliament of Canada.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REUNIFICATION OF FAMILIES- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REUNIFICATION OF FAMILIES- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are, indeed, aware of the case of Colonel Lev Ovsishcher, a Jewish refusenik who wishes to join his daughter in Israel. The Canadian government has had no involvement with this case and since it is a third country which is concerned there is little we can do in the way of representations to encourage the Soviet authorities to grant him an exit visa, much as many of us would like to help him.
Past experience has made it clear that the Soviet Union might well challenge Canada's involvement in the case and that our interests could be jeopardized in other questions with a direct Canadian interest.
Although direct intervention is not a viable option, cases such as that of Colonel Ovsischer are relevant in the context of the 1975 Helsinki Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. Basket 111 of the Final Act of this conference refers to human contacts, including the question of the freer movement of people and, in particular, with humanitarian cases of this nature, involving the reunification of families. While progress has been made in this area with the U.S.S.R., there remains, unfortunately, considerable scope for improvement. For this reason the Canadian delegation to the review conference in Madrid this autumn will press for a more forthcoming Soviet attitude toward family reunification, including such cases as that of Colonel Ovsishcher.

subtopic: NUCLEAR ENERGY-UNDERGROUND WATER DISPOSAL RESEARCH PROJECT IN MANITOBA
NUCLEAR ENERGY-UNDERGROUND WATER DISPOSAL RESEARCH PROJECT IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose tonight is to comment on the complete inadequacy, and worse, the cynicism, of the answers I received on May 12
June 2, 1980

from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) respectively.
I asked about a specific project at a specific place, the underground waste disposal research project in the vicinity of Lac du Bonnet, inquiring as to whether further work on this project might be suspended and that public hearings be held to provide a forum for the discussion of all the attendant scientific, economic, social and ethical issues.
Instead, I was blandly assured by the parliamentary secretary that the whole question of radioactive waste disposal was under active consideration with provincial governments, and particularly the governments of Ontario and Manitoba, and that he would be glad to report to the House any further developments. The parliamentary secretary's kindness in not burying me with specific or even remotely relevant information pursuant to my question, is not appreciated.
He seems to have been taking lessons from AECL in how to keep a closed mouth about difficult questions, breaking secrecy only to indulge in badly disguised propaganda, to brand concerned citizens as emotional or irrational or to admit that accidents which they previously denied have actually occurred. No more irrational, emotional or intellectually craven state of mind could be imagined than that of the promoters of nuclear energy in this country who would have Canada pursue a nuclear future without adequate public debate of any kind. Instead, they blindly advocate that the public uncritically accept their self-interested overconfidence in their own abilities and hide from appropriate political and moral discussion about this issue behind the faqade of technical expertise and the urgency of maintaining the viability of the industry, as they call it, an answer which begs the question, to say the least.
Therefore 1 call on the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to tell us now whether there will be public hearings into this research project at Lac du Bonnet, whether he can assure the House that this will indeed always be a research project and that this is not the first step in Manitoba's becoming a burial ground for Ontario's radioactive waste.
Mr. Speaker, there is already a great deal of nuclear waste in this country that needs to be safely disposed of-there is no question about that-if indeed it is possible to dispose safely of it, so research into safe disposal is in order, but only because we have arrived where we are now without choosing. It is now time to make a choice and to initiate a public debate about nuclear energy through the framework, as 1 suggest, of a moratorium, public hearings and a referendum. For this reason 1 hope the parliamentary secretary will say something
Adjournment Debate
tonight about the government's intention in this regard and not just put off the question in the way the Prime Minister did on May 12. An internal departmental review is not enough. The people must be allowed to think and to speak openly about this issue, and a conscious decision must be reached, whatever that decision may be. My personal hope is that Canadians might choose to change their way of life in such a way as to permit a more renewable, decentralized, conservationist and less risky energy future, not just for their own sakes but for the sakes of future generations. But if the people should choose otherwise, so be it. All I ask for, and all others who are interested in this issue ask for, is that we be given such a choice and that the government demonstrate that it is not simply a tool of the nuclear establishment in this country but a servant of the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NUCLEAR ENERGY-UNDERGROUND WATER DISPOSAL RESEARCH PROJECT IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since June, 1978, the Ontario and Canadian governments have been working on the first phase of a long-term project to ensure that nuclear spent fuel can be permanently disposed of in an environmentally safe manner.
Most of the geologic research, conducted under the auspices of AECL, is at present being carried out in the Ontario portion of the Canadian shield. On May 28, the Manitoba government approved the plans for the construction of an underground research laboratory near AECL's Whiteshell research establishment in the municipality of Lac du Bonnet. This new research facility is estimated to cost $7.5 million and will no doubt create many additional jobs in the area.
This is another example of how the two levels of government are capable of reaching agreement on matters of importance to all of us.
I should like to add that there has been extensive citizen involvement in the decision to locate the research laboratory in this area. For the past several months, there have been public meetings examining the question in the Whiteshell area. A citizens' liaison group formed by the reeve of the rural municipality of Lac du Bonnet found, according to the reeve, that between 96 per cent and 98 per cent of the citizens in the area approved of the project. A total of five local municipal councils passed resolutions approving AECL's plans for research in the area, and on May 7, the municipality of Lac du Bonnet informed the Manitoba government that it supported the AECL proposal. Contrary to critics' charges of a lack of citizen participation, the public is informed and is an integral part of the decision-making process.

June 2, 1980
We can all be proud of our country's unique contribution in the area of nuclear energy. In a world of decreasing energy sources and increasing energy costs, Canadians find themselves at the forefront of one of the most technologically advanced fields. We must continue our efforts to ensure that adequate energy sources are available to all in the future. I am certain that all members support accurate and timely scientific
research to ensure the continued development of our full energy potential.
